speechtext:
Hon. members will have noticed press reports of the unfortunate delay of the R.M.S. Empress of Australia, as a result of fog and ice encountered in the north Atlantic. I am glad, however, to be able to inform the house., that the Empress of Australia is now proceeding at full speed and is expected to arrive at Quebec in time to enable their majesties to land at 10.30 on Wednesday morning. The full program at Quebec, originally scheduled for Monday, May 15, will be carried out on Wednesday, the 17th.
Similarly, the program originally planned for Tuesday, including the stop at Three Rivers and the ceremonies at Montreal, will be carried out on Thursday next.
It is expected that the royal train will arrive m Ottawa on Friday, May 19, as originally arranged for Wednesday. Some rearrangement of the Ottawa program will have to be made. At present I am unable to inform the house of the detailed changes. It is expected that the ceremony of royal assent will take place on Friday as originally planned. The state dinner will take place on Friday evening and the parliamentary dinner on Saturday evening.	.	.
Hon. members will appreciate the difficulties which have resulted from the unfortunate and unpredictable delay to the Empress of Australia. I am, however, able to assure the house that every effort is being made by the interdepartmental committee so to rearrange the program as not to disappoint those in the different parts of the country who have made long and careful preparations for the reception of the king and queen. It is hoped that it will be possible for the interdepartmental committee to make later to-day a detailed announcement of the rearranged program.
I am afraid that is as far as I am able to give the house information at the moment. The circumstance that their majesties will not arrive in Ottawa until Friday will make possible the sitting of this house on Thursday, and it is the intention of the government to have the house sit on Thursday.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UN MATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES

speechtext: Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 93, to authorize the raising, by way of loan, of certain sums of money for the public service.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UN MATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
This bill can be divided into two parts. First it provides that:
The governor in council may, in addition to the sums now remaining unborrowed and negotiable of the loans authorized by parliament by any act heretofore passed, raise by
way of loan, under the provisions of The Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, 1931, by the issue and sale or pledge of securities of Canada, in such form, for such separate sums, at such rate of interest and upon such other terms and conditions as the governor in council may approve, such sum or sums of money as may be required, not to exceed in the whole the sum of seven hundred and fifty million dollars, for paying or redeeming the whole or any portion of loans or obligations of Canada,
It is the intention of the government by the issue of new securities to pay off or redeem maturing obligations of Canada, and to borrow money on the security of Canada for purchasing and withdrawing unmatured securities of Canada, and for public works and general purposes. We can deal with this bill by dividing it into two parts-the money required for retiring loans, and that required for public works and general purposes.
I moved an amendment to the resolution asking the government to issue $600,000,000 to retire Canada's obligations as mentioned in this resolution. At that time I asked the minister a number of questions which I should like to have had answered. I should like to know why that money was borrowed in the first place, and what can we as a parliament point to and say to the people that those are the assets that we have to show for the expenditure of this money. Why is it that no reserve was set up to retire these bonds as they fell due? Why is it that we must continually refund and go progressively into debt? The Minister of Finance declares that there are only two ways by which this government can secure money: one by borrowing, and the other by taxation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UN MATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: My hon. friend is misquoting me. I named a third way which is worse than the others.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UN MATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
I asked the minister whether there was no other way of raising money except by borrowing or through taxation, and the minister replied, "that is right." Of course he may have another way that he claims is worse, but I should like to have an answer to these questions. To whom do we actually owe this money? How was this debt created in the first place? A great deal of false information is being spread throughout the length and breadth of this country by bankers and their associates. They are telling the people all kinds of claptrap and buncombe; I never heard the like in all my life. The other day I was talking to a banker who has been engaged in that business for twenty years. He claimed that all money has come into existence because gold has been mined; that from the mining of gold we have brought money into existence; that the money based
Loan oj $750,000,000

upon this gold has become the deposits of the people and that banks lend the deposits of the people to individuals and to governments.
Nothing is further from the truth. Some of us assert that banks can create assets for themselves out of nothing, out of thin air, by the use of a fountain pen. Many laugh at that statement; but let us go into it. We will say the government goes to the bank with a thousand dollar bond and asks the bank to issue credit against that bond. Does the bank lend the savings of the people which it has on deposit? It absolutely does not. It creates SI,000 by the stroke of a fountain pen, and that SI ,000 is placed to the credit of the government of Canada. The bank puts that thousand dollar bond in its portfolio. The government has a deposit of $1,000 against which it can write cheques; then when the money is spent there is $1,000 on deposit in the commercial banks belonging to the people of this country, $1,000 of newly created credit, not the savings of the people. It is true that this $1,000 is a liability of the bank, but the bank has an asset of $1,000 in the form of a government bond. That bond is a revenue producing asset, and the banks hold $1,400,000,000 worth of government securities, revenue producing assets which they created by the simple expedient of using a fountain pen. It is true that they have created liabilities in the form of deposits in the commercial banks, belonging to various people in Canada; but to go back to the illustration of the thousand dollar bond and the liability of the bank in the form of $1,000 in deposit, part of that thousand dollars is taken, year by year, by the government from the people in the form of taxation to pay the interest on the bond. If the bond carried a rate of five per cent, the government would be obliged to tax the people in order to obtain the $50 to give to the bank whenever the interest fell due, thus reducing the amount of the people's deposits to the extent necessary to recover the interest due on the bond. So that the bank has a revenue producing asset, and at the end of a few years the bank would secure the face value of the bond in the form of interest, which it would use for its own purposes.
How are we going to pay off that bond? How are we going to redeem that debt of $1,000? Under the present system of taxation, or as an alternative-borrowing-we know we cannot borrow ourselves out of debt-the government would have to tax $1,000 away from the Canadian people, reducing their deposits by that amount. No

wonder the banks are anxious that the government should not tax the people to pay them off. They know that if the government taxed the people sufficiently to retire the outstanding obligations of this country, it would create national bankruptcy and would destroy the revenue producing assets of the bank. Why, if the government were to tax that $1,000 away from the people's deposits and give it to the banks, the banks would surrender the bond to the government, who would tear it up, and the banks would have to destroy the $1,000 cheque that they would receive in payment of the bond.
To support my contention may I say that many of the outstanding monetary reformers and administrators in the United States make the same contention. In the Congressional Record of the United States, under the heading Constitutional Money and Government Money Control, I find the extension of some remarks by Hon. Knute Hill, in the House of Representatives, who placed on record a radio broadcast in which Mr. Binderup, a former congressman of the United States, said:
Mr. Binderup. Right you are. Yes, truly, truth is stranger than fiction. We are basing our money on the people's debts. If we pay our debts, our money disappears, and we will all go broke. And if we don't pay our debts, the sheriff takes all we have and we will also go broke; so, in principle, it merely means that we are dammed if we do and dammed if we don't. Isn't that so?
Mr. Voorhis.
Who was also a congressman.
Yes, Binderup; you are absolutely right. If Uncle Sam and all the rest of us paid ou-r debts, there would then not be one dollar in circulation except our old reliable Abraham Lincoln coin money and our silver. The bulk of our money consists of bank deposits created by the banks for the explicit purpose of making loans. By the same token the payment of those loans wipes out the deposits and, in effect, destroys that much of our money. Under our present monetary system, the people are definitely between two fires, a money famine on the one hand and increasing debt on the other.
And in another broadcast of the same nature which was read into the Congressional Record you will find this by Professor Irving Fisher of Yale university:
Professor Fisher. Years of study have convinced me that the depression has been primarily a monetary matter. The simple failure to have a sound and stable monetary system has been the most fundamental reason for business and bank failures, foreclosures, bankruptcies, and unemployment-in a word, for the depression. It was the depression, the pressure of starving and disillusioned men and women, which mainly caused and still causes the great world upheavals-economic, political, social, and even religious.
Senator Norris. But how can our money system have such a powerful influence?

Loan of $750,000,000
Professor Fisher. Simply because money has become a prime necessity in our civilization. Without it. goods cannot be sold and will not be produced. There may be crying need for the necessities of life; there may be all the iron, coal, lumber, and other raw materials used for manufacturing; there may be millions of able-bodied men anxious to work, yet, if there is no money there is no production; there is unemployment and starvation. You have witnessed all this. Scarcity of money is called deflation. It is just as great an evil as its opposite, superabundance of money, called inflation. Inflation makes booms; deflation makes depressions.
And he goes on to contend that banks create money out of nothing, that they do not lend the savings of the people. When a private individual goes to a bank he does not borrow the savings of his friends. Professor Fisher says this;
The greatest confusion comes from a general lack of understanding of what we use for money. Our principal money has no existence whatever, except in the figures on the ledgers of our commercial banks. We call it bank credit. It is the credit balances in the checking accounts of the individuals, firms and corporations of the nation. It is created and destroyed by the commercial banks. When you borrow $500 from a commercial bank, it is quite different from borrowing $500 from a friend. When you borrow from a friend, the transaction adds $500 to your cash and takes $500 from the cash of your friend. The total sum of money in circulation is not changed, but borrowing $500 from a commercial bank is an entirely different transaction. The bank creates the $500 credit which it enters on its ledgers, and y9u enter on the stub of your checkbook. It is, in effect. $500 of new money. The purchasing power ot the nation has increased $500. It is almost as if the bank had printed $500 of new bank notes to lend to you. Actually, there is no such money in the bank, but only that pen-and-ink record on the bank's books. It is merely a promise of the bank to furnish you $500 of currency and coin on demand. You transfer the title to that promise by drawing checks against it just as if it were real money, and those to whom you pay these checks accept them as money. We may therefore call these promises checkbook money, as contrasted with real or pocketbook money. The important fact, however, is that, call it what you will, this $500 you have borrowed is new money. It never existed before you borrowed it. Your act of borrowing added $500 to the circulating medium of the United States.
Senator Norris: What really happened when you borrowed that $500 is that you and the bank swapped promises. You promised to pay the bank $500 in 3 months with interest, and in return for this promise the bank promised to furnish $500 in money upon demand at any time. You really do not want the actual money ordinarily. You really want this credit upon which you can draw cheeks and transfer to others. The recipients of your checks do not ordinarily want the money in actual cash. Ihey, too, want the credit, which they in turn can transfer by check, and so this credit continues to circulate in the continuous transfer of goods and services and serves just as actual currency and coin. And yet, as you have stated, it has no actual existence excepting in figures upon the ledgers of the banks.
We have suggested that the government should issue $600,000,000 to retire the portion of outstanding obligations falling due in the coming year. But the government is of the opinion that that would create inflation. We realize that simply to issue $600,000,000, without controlling the creation of credit, which is a power in the hands of the banks at the present time, would create inflation. And so we have advocated that the government direct the banks to increase their cash reserve.
There are many students of money in the United States. Those students are found not only among the members of the Senate and the House of Representatives, but among economists in business and professors in the universities. They have even formed an association known as the Monetary Reform Association, in which are found some of the outstanding men of the United States. They have advocated what is known as the one hundred per cent money idea. I should like to put on record the facts in connection with this one hundred per cent money idea, as explained by Robert L. Owen, former chairman of the committee on banking in the United States. At page 62 of The National Economy and The Banking System of the United States he says-
Mr. DUNNING; Mr. Speaker, I rise to a point of order. I do not wish to limit the debate; certainly it cannot be said that there has been any limitation, because this matter has been before the house on six previous occasions and at each time was debated fully.
I now call your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the rule respecting reiteration and repetition of argument, inasmuch as the debate on a bill the other day was ruled to be continuous on the whole of the bill. The arguments now being made-in fact some of the exact words- have been repeated at least three or four times in the debate. While I know the hon. member wishes to take full advantage of the rules so far as they apply to liberty of speech, I submit that that very fact makes hon. members subject to the rules and to the rights of other hon. members.
I would call your attention, Mr. Speaker, to citation 287, page 93 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms:
287. Mr. Speaker or the Chairman, after having called the attention of the house, or of the committee, to the conduct of a member who persists in irrelevance, or tedious repetition either in his own argument, or of arguments used by other members in the debate, may direct him to discontinue his speech.
I rise at this stage to speak, not particularly with respect to the hon. member alone, but because it is evident that we are in for a

seventh repetition of similar arguments and similar facts. I ask you, sir, to consider the matter.

speechtext:
Then I shall just read this into the record, and in that way I will not be repeating myself.
One Hundred Per Cent Reserves It has heretofore been pointed out that the power of the privately owned banks, state and national, to expand the money supply by loans and contract the money supply by liquidating the loans, or requiring the loans paid has been the means of repeated booms and depressions in the United States.
In order to put an end to this destabilizing influence and power, many economists now believe with Professor Irving Fisher of Yale that the national and state banks should be required to have one hundred per cent reserves with the Federal Reserve banks against their demand bank deposits. The effect of this would be:
1.	The inability of the banks to cause booms and depressions by the indefensible expansion and contraction of credit.
2.	The absolute stability in the security of the demand bank deposits all of which could be liquidated instantly on the demand of the demand bank depositors.
3.	By this method the banks would have perfect security against the possibility of any sudden demand.
4.	The banks would still have the money arising from savings accounts and time deposits which they could invest, or could loan for business purposes.
5.	The banks would still have the right to obtain loans from the Federal Reserve banks or sell to the Federal Reserve banks commercial bills and real estate loans on long time.

6.	The banks of course would have the earnings from handling deposit accounts, both as to number and in the volume of such accounts.
7.	The banks would have stability in the solvency of their borrowers and stability in the value of their investments, and would automatically cease to finance speculative operations on tne security and commodity exchanges under a properly ordered system.
In addition to these advantages to the banks tne United States would have the advantage of acquiring through the Reserve banks the United States bonds, which the banks and pubhc hold, by the payment of these bonds when they fall due or are sold to the Reserve banks m credit of the Federal Reserve banks. Under this system the Federal Reserve banks would gradually acquire the public debt, save the interest on such bonds and the amortization charges, and therefore greatly facilitate the balancing of the budget.
,, -The 100 per cent reserves required against the demand bank deposits would make it impossible for the banks to create an inflation of the money supply of the United States with its destabilizing influence. The banks at present have in cash and bonds a 100 per cent reserve against their demand deposits.
If the government really has control over money and credit day by day, week by week, and month by month, surely it can prevent any inflation on the part of commercial banks.
I desire to move an amendment to the motion, as follows:
That all the words after the word "that" in the motion be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"In the opinion of this house, it is expedient that the governor in council should be authorized to raise by the issue of currency and/or credit through the Bank of Canada an amount not to exceed $200,000,000 for public works and general purposes."
I am not unmindful of the promise made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that when any individual made a suggestion to parliament, the matter would be given prompt attention and efficient direction. I am anxious that this amendment should be debated. I do not think it is sufficient that the minister should rise in his place and say that it would create uncontrolled inflation. We know that the borrowing of money under the present system is defended by orthodox economists. I intend to deal with some of the statements which have been made by orthodox economists in attempting to discredit the monetary reformers of this and other countries. They want to know whether this money is going to be printing press or fiat money. They continually try to alarm the people by such statements. The fact is that our present system is based upon printing press money and we are working under a fiat money system at the present time. Then they become greatly concerned about what the redemption is to be, they want to know

Loan of $750,000,000
with what we are going to redeem the money. Money is redeemed every time a citizen is prepared to give a commodity or services for it. The only value of money is its possibility of transfer for goods and services. _
If the money we have at the present time is not made of rubber, it surely has acted as though it were. We have had changes in value from year to year; we have had no stabilized value in terms of commodities or services, and this has caused all kinds of hardships for the producers, the wage earners and the debtors of this country. Surely we can find some way to stabilize the value of our money and prevent the terrible effects of the unstabilized dollar of the past.
I should like the minister to answer some of the questions that we have directed to him in the past. I should like to hear from him just what effect the issuing of this $200,000,000 by the government, instead of borrowing it and adding to our national debt, would have upon the country as a whole. The minister contends that we have an easy money policy in this country, and I should like to know just what that easy money policy has accomplished. What effect has that easy money policy had upon the position of the unemployed? Has it benefited the unemployed of this country? Has it benefited the primary producers of this country, the wheat growers of western Canada? Has it benefited the wage earners of this country? Has it assisted private individuals, municipalities and the provincial and federal governments in meeting their debt obligations?

We have never had any adequate explanation from any Liberal in the house of just how the Liberal government intended to carry out that policy. I am still waiting for an explanation; none has been given. What did the leaders of the Liberal party mean when they said that they would issue currency and credit in terms of private and public need. Perhaps I should not have used the word "need"; I should have said "requirement," because there was quite a discussion in the house whether the Prime Minister used the word "need" or "requirement." The people of Canada, I and others are all anxious to hear the detailed plan of the Liberal government to abolish poverty in this country as was promised by the Prime Minister, and just what effect this easy money policy has had, and just what the Bank of Canada is doing for the people of Canadh- or are they just lackeys for the commercial banks? Are they continuing the policy of restricting credit and permitting the destruction of money by the commercial banks in times of depression, or has the central bank control over the entire money system of this country. We should like to be shown whether we are right or wrong. If we are right, we expect to receive the support of intelligent members of parliament.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UN MATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there seems to be a certain amount of resentment on the part of several hon. members because of the emphasis we in this *corner are placing on the subject of money. Personally I do not think that resentment is in the least justified. Surely all hon. members and the people of the country at large must realize by now that the major obstacle in dealing with our problems is the present monetary policy. Personally I am not going to indulge in undue repetition of material that has already been placed on Hansard. I shall rather endeavour to say a few things that have not been said thus far.
I am convinced that there is no more important subject which can be discussed in this house or in any parliament in any country of the world than monetary policy. Every phase of our national life, every activity in which we indulge privately or publicly depends absolutely upon the medium of exchange. What is the use of talking about trade or public works or any form of enterprise if you have not at your command an adequate financial system? You can accomplish nothing in this world unless you have an adequate monetary policy. Everything we do, every phase of our activities, depends on the use *of the medium of exchange, and if that medium of exchange and the policy under which it is issued does not conform to or is not in harmony with what we are trying to do, we can never attain our objectives. We are not living in a barter age in which we can swap goods for goods. That day has gone by.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UN MATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: The Germans are doing it to-day, are they not?

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UN MATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
No, they are not. True, there is an exchange of goods, from one point of view, but it involves the use of tickets of some kind, whether it be cheques or bills for the transfer of goods. Undoubtedly it involves the use of some medium of exchange. So, Mr. Speaker, I do not think that any criticism levelled at us in this corner for emphasizing monetary policy is justified.
I wish to protest on two scores in particular against the principle of Bill No. 93, to borrow an additional $750,000,000. The first score on which I protest is that the bill seeks to perpetuate the criminal practice of permitting a private monopoly to issue the medium of exchange. The medium of exchange I consider to be the crown's prerogative- indeed, the most sacred of the crown's prerogatives, because the life and destiny of every individual in the nation is absolutely dependent on the monetary policy that is pursued. Rothschild in 1790 said: "Give me
the power to create the money of a nation and I care not who makes its laws." That statement emphasizes the fact that those who control the money control the nation. If a private monopoly has the control of money, parliament should know it, because when that condition prevails parliament can do nothing to control the affairs of the nation. To-day our medium of exchange is still issued, not by parliament but by a private monopoly. This most sacred prerogative of the crown is in the control of a private monopoly. I regard that as a capital crime.
Judging by some remarks that have been made in this house, we who advocate the government issue of money have been looked upon as heretics. In fact, the shoe is on the other foot; those who are insisting that the government shall not issue money but that a private monopoly should be allowed to do so are the real heretics. All money should be issued by the government; every cent of money put into circulation should be government money. Our national conscience has become so calloused that to-day we do not even distinguish between right and wrong. We imply by our statements that a private monopoly should have the right to issue money, but that the government should not. If governments issue a dollar, it is inflation. We must bestir ourselves and wake up to the fact that the putting of money into circulation is a crown prerogative, something that belongs to the government, to the state; and no private monopoly should be permitted to issue even a five-cent piece. That is the first score on which I protest against this bill. It perpetuates the practice of permitting a private monopoly to issue the medium of exchange.
The question of policy under which the medium of exchange is issued is another matter entirely, which we can debate; but as to the government's right to issue and put into circulation the medium of exchange, I do not think there should be any debate at all. It should be taken for granted that the government is the only authority that should have the privilege of issuing the medium of exchange.
The second ground on which I protest against this bill is that it places another mathematical impossibility before the Canadian people. If we pass the bill authorizing the government to borrow another $750,000,000- and this is true of all bills which have permitted such action-we are simply adding more weight to the already mathematically impossible problem which the Canadian people are expected to face. Those who criticize the social credit philosophy have
Loan of #750,000,000

frequently suggested that we advocate a weird sort of economy in which we expect two plus two to equal six, but that is exactly what we are expecting of the people of Canada under the present policy. Under present circumstances it is mathematically impossible for the people of the country to pay interest on money. The banks are the ones who expect two plus two to equal six. All that is created in the way of money is a loan, regardless of whether it is a loan to governments or a loan to private individuals. An amount of money equivalent to interest which is expected of the public on private or government loans is never created. It is merely the principle that is created, and if the people are expected to pay interest, they can do so only by going further into debt at the rate of interest charged for the use of money. The fact that our debts have progressively increased rather than decreased is proof positive that this is so.
The borrowing of this additional S750,000,000 will simply mean that the people of Canada will be expected to meet an obligation equivalent to the interest charged on the money, no matter how small or how great it is, and that is a mathematical impossibility.

Every one who uses money, who obtains loans, owes to the banks more than he can pay back, so that the collective obligation of the people to the banking institutions is greater than the people can mathematically repay. I see no reason at all why we should have a national debt.

speechtext:
Any debt at all. Actually
in a country in which we have the physical resources and the resources of human energy and skill, I see no reason why we should be obliged to go into debt. Anything we wish to accomplish costs only these things, the physical materials and the human energy and skill, together with the time involved in production, whether what is produced be foodstuffs or clothing or shelter or public works or a railway system or the requirements for waging war. In the final analysis, the only cost of doing any of these things consists in the material, the time, and the human energy and skill necessary. If in the past we have provided these things and have met our obligations collectively in a physical way at all times, why should our money system, our book-keeping system, indicate to-day that we are in debt? What is wrong is that our banking system, our monetary policy, our book-keeping system, does not reflect the facts. Every cent of the medium of exchange that we need in order to engage in enterprises, whether public or private, is issued by a private monopoly, issued as debt, and we are expected to pay back more than we are mathematically able to pay. Consequently, because of the monetary policy, we are forced into debt. There is no way out. Yet we have met all the real costs.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UN MATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES

Will the hon. member

speechtext: Do I understand that the hon. member goes as far in inveighing against the present system as to advocate a policy which would cancel existing debts?

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UN MATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
No. I am not dealing with the manner in which we should settle our debts; I am dealing with the principle of creating a financial debt as opposed to the costs involved in carrying on enterprise, whether public or private. The question of how to settle these debts I am not going to discuss at this time. I am trying to point out that there is no reason why we should be going into debt for another $750,000,000 or whatever amount it is going to be. We can afford the costs of book-keeping, the cost of issuing this money. Money to-day is simply a question of book-keeping, of figures in a book. We have book-keeping services, we have those skilled in the art of bookkeeping, we have an excellent banking system so far as the institution and methods used in the book-keeping are concerned. We can afford the costs of conducting the money

Loan of $750,000,000
system. The only costs are human labour, skill and the consumption of material. We are meeting those costs from day to day If we wish to carry on a huge program of public works, we have the necessary labour; we have the machines, the materials, all the physical things necessary. Then why should we not set up a book-keeping system that will reflect these facts, and when we have built a road, say that that road is paid for?- because when that road is built it is paid for. There are no further costs. The rest is merely book-keeping. We can afford to do in this country exactly what we can provide the physical material and the human skill and energy to do; that is the only cost of doing anything. Why, then, can we not engage in a system of public works, of hard-surfacing all our roads, completing the trans-Canada highway and making it a real highway? Why can we not carry on a large system of public works? We have all the real physical requirements. In every province we have plenty of material, and idle men and machinery. But just for the want of tickets we are unable to bring these things about.
We should carry on a slum clearance program. We have the building material; we ship millions of feet of lumber out of this country every year; why should we not use it in the erection of houses to provide for our own people? We are shipping many things out of this country which we could use here, but we cannot use them simply because our policy of issuing these tickets does not conform with the needs and desires of our people. As to all the debts which have been incurred in the past, whether for public works, the waging of wars, the railway system, or anything that we have done in the way of public or private enterprise, every one of them should be marked paid in full; they were all paid in physical materials and human skill and effort. Why should we, just because we have not adopted the proper policy in connection with our national book-keeping system, say that we are in debt, when actually we are not? The war was paid for when the war was over. We provided all our share of the cost of that war at the time. Why should we and our children and our children's children be obliged to provide a rake-off for a private issuer of the tickets and the book-keeping service that we needed during the war?

speechtext: Could we deal in the same way with our individual debts? There is nothing I should like so much as to do it by book-keeping.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UN MATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES

That is all you do, anyway. I am not suggesting that it is merely the figures in the books that meet the debt obligation,
but the figures in the books reflect what takes place physically. The figures in the books to-day are not doing that. We have met the costs, but the figures say we are in debt.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UN MATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Change the books.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UN MATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES

Absolutely, we are asking that that be done. Hon. members opposite told the people of the country that they were going to do that, but they have not done it. That is all we ask the government to do-change the book-keeping system and make it reflect the facts. If the cost has been met, the books must say that the bills are paid in full. If the book-keeping system is not changed, we shall have to change the book-keepers.
In my opinion the first duty of this government is to restore to parliament the crown prerogative. Whether the Prime Minister in the last election stated that in so many words is difficult to say, but certainly the people drew that inference when he said that until the control of the issue of currency and credit is restored to the government and recognized as its most conspicuous and sacred responsibility, all talk of the sovereignty of parliament and of democracy is idle and futile.
If one examines those words carefully, of course it may be said that there is nothing there to indicate that parliament should issue money. It merely says "until the control of the issue of currency and credit is restored." I believe that the Prime Minister played up-

It is a satisfactory payment as between one individual and another; it is a medium of accounting, if you like. But a medium of exchange is something which passes readily from hand to hand; it does not require to be paid into a bank and be cashed and another one issued. A medium of exchange is something which passes around freely, carrying at all times on its face a stable value. That cannot be said of a cheque on my account in favour of my hon. friend. It is all right in his hands, because in accepting it he has confidence that he can get legals for it at the bank, because he believes I have an account there; but he could not continue passing that cheque around with endorsement after endorsement on it, using it as a hand to hand medium of exchange in the proper sense of the term.

Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to enter into a discussion of monetary reform matters, because these things can be done at another time and place.- Before the banking and commerce committee last Wednesday I endeavoured to discuss the basis of a financial system. However, we have before us a bill, and an amendment thereto which, since it has not been questioned, I must conclude is at the moment in order and open for discussion.
The original proposal of the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Landeryou) was that 750,000,000 of new dollars might be issued in order to retire the bonds maturing, to retire certain treasury bills, and to provide a balance which might be utilized for the provision of public works. I thought then, and I think now, that if the words "and general purposes" at the end of the amendment mean that any part of the amount men-

Loan of $750,000,000
tioned in the amendment shall be used to retire bonds now maturing, it may not have the result which I am sure hon. members supporting the amendment would wish it to have. In other words the portion of the issue used for that purpose would pass immediately into the hands of persons and financial institutions who would have no use for it other than to place it in their bank accounts for reinvestment in other securities of perhaps a similar nature. If they sought these fields of investment, the net result would be a rise in the monetary value of government bonds offered for sale on the open market, and of other gilt-edged securities. When these became exhausted in number the investor might turn to some other less remunerative or less desirable field, and if we proceeded all the way down the line the result might be a speculative boom. There is no guarantee that that portion of the amount first mentioned as $750,000,000, or the amount mentioned in the amendment as $200,000,000, would benefit the workers and farmers to the extent to which such an issue might be beneficial to them.
Having said that, let me say that I am not opposed to the proposal before us on the ground upon which many would oppose it, namely, that it would mean inflation. That argument certainly does not frighten me, because I am convinced that we are suffering from a severe deflation of prices and employment. The fall in the value of our primary commodities which has taken place in the past few years must be arrested. The price level of our primary commodities must be raised, otherwise our whole economy will suffer. When I say that, I realize that money has some basis in fact, some basis in real goods and services. I think the mistake our friends often make when discussing monetary reform is, as I have said before, that they tend to mistake the shadow for the substance.
I seldom tell a story in this house, but I heard a good one the other day which I think I should repeat. A farmer in Alberta was taking a lot of hay tc a nearby village last autumn. A friend stopped him and said, "John, I see you are taking a lot of hay to town. Are you selling it for cash or credit?" John said, "I am selling it on credit." His friend then asked, 'Are you not going to lose a lot of money?" John replied, "No, but I may lose a lot of hay." I think that illustrates the point that must be understood when we discuss money.

The only way that demand can be met is by the provision of goods or the provision of services.
I am not saying that our friends in bringing monetary matters to the attention of the House of Commons are not rendering a valuable service. I think they are, because there are many things in connection with our economic affairs that we ought to understand better than we do. Much thought should be given to improving our banking and monetary systems so that they will serve the nation as a whole rather than a comparatively few people. Therefore I am not opposing the principle of the issue of national money by the Bank of Canada under the direction of this parliament; I am only opposing any suggestion that we can issue unlimited amounts at any particular time.

If we are going to issue new money, let us place it in the hands of those who must spend it on consumer goods, such as food, clothing, homes, and so on. As I said on Wednesday before the banking and commerce committee, if we are going to pump it in at all, let us pump it in at the bottom rather than into the stagnant pool at the top. If our object is to stimulate our economy, let us stimulate it where the stimulation will most beneficially affect our economy.
Our two most pressing problems at the moment are unemployment and the low prices received for agricultural products. To pay many millions of dollars to bondholders cannot ameliorate these problems to any appreciable degree. The stimulation of secondary production which would result in greater employment and a consequent demand for farm products would depend entirely upon the reinvestment of these funds by private capitalists and corporations. " Free of debt " is really a misnomer. The moment a dollar is issued by the government it is a demand for a dollar's worth of someone's goods or services. Somewhere in our economy someone will have to pay a dollar's worth of commodities or goods to me, the demand for which I hold at the moment, and which is their debt to me temporarily. Consequently I am speaking of our dollar as being free of interest. As I said, I am not opposed to such an issue to finance a comprehensive program of works, housing or even to improve our social services. This money would pass immediately into the hands of persons who need more food, more clothes, more furniture, more houses, more of everything that industry and agriculture produces. This in turn, I believe, would improve the demand for milk, butter, cheese, eggs and other agricultural products, and, therefore, benefit the farmer. I take it that these are the groups which suffer most to-day under our present economic chaos.
It seems to me that we should also keep in mind the fact that when the money had been spent the nation would have something to show for it. The nation would have public works, houses and services, to the value of the sum issued, while the farmer and the unemployed would have furniture, food, and many of the amenities of life that they now lack. Municipalities would be able to improve their tax position through having arrears paid, while lending institutions would benefit by the repayment of loans in full or in part. Manufacturers and retailers would benefit, and I believe our whole economy would be stimulated. If we are going to try the experiment of issuing interest-free money, then let it be tried in the manner which is most likely to do the most good.

speechtext:
When the house rose at one o'clock I was discussing what I thought the effect of the issue of, say $100,000,000 worth of new money would be upon the economy. Some, of course, will argue also that this would depreciate our Canadian currency in terms of foreign exchange, and that Canada is an exporter of goods. In my opinion, there are circumstances under which such depreciation would actually benefit the Canadian producer. Recently we have seen a slight depreciation of the pound sterling in terms of Canadian dollars, and in 1932 such a depreciation occurred to a very large extent, I believe at one time the pound sterling fell in value to such an extent that the exchange was about $3.25 in our money, and that was
Loan of $750,000,000

a disaster to the Canadian farmer-not only the western farmer, but the entire farming community of Canada.
Depreciation of the dollar in terms of foreign exchange would give one class of producers, those who produce export commodities, a larger return for their goods in terms of Canadian currency, provided, of course, the depreciation were not too great. I notice that the Australian government is considering the fixing of a set price for Australian wheat at 3s. lOd. per bushel. If we remember that we have a normal exchange rate of $4.87 to the pound and the Australian currency gives them 480 halfpennies to the pound, we can make a comparison using the halfpenny as a cent, and under normal exchange conditions 3s. lOd. would give them 92 halfpennies or cents with which to retire their own internal debt with their own internal currency. But when we translate the proposed price of wheat in Australia into Canadian money at current rates of exchange, that is, 65 cents, we are neglecting the effect upon the domestic economy of Australia; consequently I believe that if there were some depreciation in our currency overseas as a result of the issue of additional currency in Canada it would at least benefit our Canadian producers.
The difficulty under our present system is that the manipulation of currency results in increasing or decreasing returns to various classes in the community, and at the present moment the farmer suffers from low prices and the worker from unemployment while those in receipt of fixed incomes from bonds, mortgages, securities and so on are able to obtain more goods for money expended. Of course, depreciation, if it occurred, would tend to take something from the latter group and give it to the former. Again we are faced with a problem of choice.

accrue from depreciation outweigh the other factors which the minister has in mind. I say, therefore, that we are faced with a problem of choice.

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UN MATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext: Does my hon. friend consider the tariff raising effects of currency depreciation?

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UN MATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
No, I did not consider the effect upon the tariff. Probably there is an argument there against what I am saying. Still, I believe that all these risks are worth taking if we can do the two things that we need to do at the present time. In other words, we have this choice: either employment for the unemployed and better prices for the producer, or doing away with some of the privileges which another group in our society enjoy to-day. I believe that eventually it would improve even their position, because improved economic conditions would improve conditions for all the people. But until that improvement comes I will admit that inflation-if it should prove to be inflation, though I do not think it would; it would be rather reflation-would reduce the return to some groups in the community.
I am willing to admit, in the course of an argument such as this, that you cannot get something for nothing, although the redistribution of wealth which would result from large expenditures on public works, financing directly and effectively increased consumption among the workers and benefiting the farmers, would eventually result in improved conditions generally. My argument is that instead of placing money in at the top to retire bonds we should endeavour to finance consumption, and that would improve conditions generally throughout the economy.
I said, too, that improved conditions would improve our tax position. I mean not only municipal taxation but the tax position of the country; because it would enable our national treasury to collect more money from those to whom it would eventually flow, particularly if it were accompanied by more steeply graded income tax and death duties. If we owned the entire banking system, an operation of this sort would be easier; but we do not own either the chartered banks or any large segment of our economy; hence we must rely on taxation to recover the national issue in order to reissue national money in the future. This is something we sometimes overlook when discussing monetary reform. In other words you cannot issue money indefinitely without providing some means of recovering at least the major part of the issue, and that has to be done usually by taxation. You could not

Loan oj $750,000,000
keep on issuing new national money without recovering a substantial part of it, because if you did your economy would be in other difficulties.
The raising of the total national income enables a government to raise more revenues by taxation, and the experience of the United States in the last few years has shown this. There they raised annually the national income by some $30,000,000,000 between 1932 and 1937, enabling the government to collect more revenue by $4,400,000,000 annually. In Canada, incidentally, we have benefited from what they have done in the United States, making it, in the eyes of our government, unnecessary to do what they did there.
I would point out also that our circulating medium to-day has not increased-I mean our active circulating medium. There has been no increase in recent years over 1929 and our price level at the moment, in terms of the 1926 price level, if you take that at 100, is about 73. Consequently I would argue that if we brought that up to the 1926 level, 27 per cent more, we should have, not inflation, but simply reflation to that level. We are frequently told that the present currency is all that we require to carry our present credit needs, and that the issue of $100,000,000 would increase the reserves of the chartered banks, and that all that it would really do would be to broaden the base so that they might issue another billion dollars' worth of loans, and so on. That may be true. On the other hand I think this is true, that to-day private enterprise will not do the things which should be done in order to relieve unemployment. That is largely because the banks, as private institutions anxious to preserve their profit basis, are unwilling to lend money to private enterprise to carry on the work, particularly what is usually called the unprofitable work, which needs to .be done. So that if private enterprise will neither invest its own savings nor borrow from the banks, a public issue for public works is in my opinion fully justified.
I did not expect this matter to come up to-day, and I have not had an opportunity of looking up a statement which was made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) in the house earlier in the session. I am not sure of the exact amount, but I believe that on one occasion he said we could issue an additional amount of currency without impairing our gold standard basis.

That objection, then, cannot be raised to what it is proposed to do. Of course I have mentioned as I passed along
the dangers, which I fully appreciate; but I believe that in the situation in which we are to-day, with a choice before us, the choice which is suggested by the subamendment is well worth trying. I am therefore going to move, seconded by Mr. Douglas (Weyburn):
That the amendment be amended by striking out the amount "two hundred million dollars" and substituting the amount "one hundred million dollars"; and further, that the words "for general purposes" be deleted from the last line and the words "during the current financial' year" be substituted therefor.
I make these alterations first of all because I think that if we are to issue an amount of money of this description it should be issued definitely for a purpose, and that purpose ought to be for public works, to go in at the bottom as consumers' purchasing power instead of into the stagnant pool of bank deposits at the top. The amendment includes the words, " for general purposes." That may mean anything. It may mean for the retirement of debt, and I should be opposed to issuing money for the retirement of debt when wre need large sums of money for public works.
I would also say that the amendment should set a period of time during which this money should be spent. The amendment does not deal with that, and the bill provides for an expenditure of money over several years-I have just forgotten how many. Therefore to leave the issue of this money for a specific purpose to be spread over, we will say, a few years, would not do what I want to see done. The government might spend only $10,000,000 this year and leave the other $190,000,000 to be spent in subsequent years. I want to see the amount authorized definitely earmarked to deal with the present unemployment and the low price level of primary commodities. That is why I have moved the subamendment to the amendment.

Yes. As I see it, the danger of that is the same as the danger in using opium. As a medical man I know something about the opium habit. Anyone who does not and who wants to read about it can do so in that very fine story by De Quincy, Confessions of an English Opium Eater. I read it many years ago; I well remember seeing De Quincy's grave in Edinburgh when I was studying over there. In taking opium, a victim gets so that he wants to take larger and larger quantities to give him the same effect which at first he derived from a small dose. There is a similar danger in connection with the issuance of fiat money. One issue goes out and undoubtedly seems to do good; it picks up the patient, it revives business and starts freer spending; there seems to be a great improvement in the patient's condition-the patient in this case being our country-and it seems reasonable to issue more as the good effect of the first dose dies down. So you get in the position where more fiat money is demanded, just as the opium eater, after he takes a dose which does not affect him so well as the last, begs for more. That is the great danger.

At the same time I am not condemning the subamendment. I do unqualifiedly condemn as beyond the realm of reason, the idea of issuing, as has been proposed once or twice in this house, and sometimes before the banking and [DOT] commerce committee, $650,000,000 or $750,000,000 worth of money.
The reason I say even the experts may be wrong is that if you look back over our monetary history, even for the last few years, you will find the changes so great that to-day we are working under a controlled or managed paper currency which even a short time ago would have been said to be absolutely impossible to work under. I do not think there can be any doubt about that. We are virtually on a fiat money basis to-day, without a doubt, on a controlled paper money basis. Not so long ago you could cash in your bills and get gold for them. I well remember that on my first visit to England, and I think on some of my subsequent visits, we had to carry a leather purse-I think I have my first one yet, a pigskin purse-in which to carry around the gold. If I remember correctly at that time there was no smaller bill than the five pound note. maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UN MATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
That is a debatable point. As a matter of fact that is why I say there is a germ of truth in the arguments of my hon. friends. I do not know how much is too much. But certainly I would say unhesitatingly that $600,000,000 or $700,000,000 in one year is too much. I do not know whether $100,000,000 would be too much. I rather think it would be. However I do not wish to be dogmatic. My hon. friends may be experts but certainly I am not an expert, and I admit it. The only reason I have never opened my mouth in the house before on the subject is that it is so complicated, and that there is so much uncertainty as to the absolute truth. Therefore I have hesitated to be dogmatic about it.
I was going to say that anyone who has studied other countries must have formed some opinions in the matter. For example, in the United States after the civil war large amounts of fiat money were issued. That money became worthless. Among some of the earliest paper money I *ever saw were confederate notes, worth nothing at all. I think we still see the odd one; I used to see them when I was a youngster. The most recent illustration, one within the memory of all of us, is found in what happened in Germany. In the early twenties Germany issued unlimited amounts of paper money. In 1923 I purchased for ten cents a German note worth a million marks-equal to $250,000 at par-and if I had waited longer I might have saved seven or eight cents on the deal. I point this out only to illustrate how worthless the paper money became.

She borrowed sufficiently after the war to pay part of them. The fact is that she made victims of other countries; for every dollar she paid out in interest and indemnity she borrowed an equal amount from the United States, England and France. And when the time came she simply handed back to those countries their own money. Then she borrowed a lot more money for the building of good roads, new buildings and all that sort of thing. She spent the money in her own land and did not pay it back. I say if we wished to repudiate our debts we would save about a hundred million dollars a year. If we repudiated only our war debts-

speechtext:
I submit that $600,000,000 issued in paper money at the present time would be inflation. I may be wrong. I am not putting myself up as being always in the right or anything of that kind. I never have done that. And I say further that my hon. friend is quite at liberty to go on arguing as he does.
This book was written by Andrew Dickson White, a fine scholar, who became Ambassador to Germany and various other countries. Speaking of the French revolution he refers particularly to the issuance of fiat money- mandats and assignats, as they were called in those days. I would point out that that paper money was not issued without backing. As a matter of fact it was issued with the backing of confiscated estates of the church and of the aristocrats of France.

speechtext: Yes. They were assets in all amounting to about a billion dollars. Those assignats and mandats were issued with a backing of that amount. And yet as a result of that issuance a most terrible condition arose in France.

speechtext: But is it not so that that was sabotaged by the issue of millions of overseas notes?

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UN MATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
No; I think France was sabotaged by the issuance of these notes. That is what happened. At first the issue stimulated -business. Then, after that improvement, things toned down. Another issue was made, and another-more and more and more was pumped into the monetary situation, with results which I shall describe when I read from the book. Even Mirabeau, one of the great men of France of that day, supported the proposal. In reading the book it is interesting to note that one
Loan of $750,000,000

of the ancestois of the du Ponts, who are now among the strong financial people of the United States, was one of the few who opposed the issuance of paper money to an unlimited extent. He fought against it, but Mirabeau, a great man at that time, advocated the issuance of it.
I do not wish to take too much time in reading. As a matter of fact I do not often read from a book in the House of Commons- either from anybody else's, or my own. My own book is quoted sufficiently by others and I do not think it is much of an argument when a man quotes others instead of presenting his own thoughts. However, I do not think I can put the argument I want to offer in phraseology better than that used by Andrew Dickson White, and I intend to read a few paragraphs from his book.
First, I should like to quote the introduction to the book, which is not by the writer:
To Americans of yesterday the name of Doctor Andrew Dickson White, university president, historian, diplomat, was a familiar one. Born in central New York November 7, 1832, the son of a successful but conscientious and public-spirited financier-
I find that language a little queer; I do not know why he uses the word " but."
-and educated at Hobart and Yale, in France and in Germany, he was at twenty-five professor of history in the university of Michigan.
That is from the introduction to his book, and I quote it to indicate that Doctor White was an outstanding authority. I shall go on now and read from the book itself, but before doing so I should like to read shortly from a foreword by Mr. John Mackay, who said:
The story of "Fiat money inflation in France" is one of great interest to legislators, to economic students, and to all business and thinking men. It records the most gigantic attempt ever made in the history of the world by a government to create an inconvertible paper currency, and to maintain its circulation at various levels of value. It also records what is perhaps the greatest of all governmental efforts-with the possible exception of Diocletian's-to enact and enforce a legal limit of commodity prices.
A little lower down:
They left behind them a legacy of moral and material desolation and woe, from which one of the most intellectual and spirited races of Europe has suffered for a century and a quarter, and will continue to suffer until the end of time. There are limitations to the powers of governments and of peoples that inhere in the constitution of things, and that neither despotisms nor democracies can overcome.
Legislatures are as powerless to abrogate moral and economic laws as they are to abrogate physical laws. They cannot convert wrong into right nor divorce effect from cause, either by parliamentary majorities, or by unity of supporting public opinion.
[Mr. Manion.l
And again:
From among an almost infinite variety, there are four great and fundamental facts that clearly emerge, namely,-
(1) Notwithstanding the fact that the paper currency issued was the direct obligation of the state, that much of it was interest bearing, and that all of it was secured upon the finest real estate in France, and that penalties in the way of fines, imprisonments and death were enacted from time to time to maintain its circulation at fixed values, there was a steady depreciation in value until it reached zero point and culminated in repudiation. The aggregate of the issues amounted to no less than the enormous and unthinkable sum of $9,500,000,000, and in the middle of 1797 when public repudiation took place, there was no less than $4,200,000,000 in face value of assignats and mandats outstanding; the loss, as always, falling mostly upon the poor and the ignorant.
In the attempt to maintain fixed values for the paper currency the government became involved in an equally futile attempt to maintain a tariff of legal prices for commodities. Here again penalties of fines, of imprisonments and of death were powerless to accomplish the end in view.
An wholesale demoralization of society took place under which thrift, integrity, humanity, and every principle of morality were thrown into the welter of seething chaos and cruelty.
The real estate upon which the paper currency was secured represented confiscations by the state of the lands of the church and of the emigrant noblemen. These lands were appraised, according to Mr. White's narrative and other authorities, at $1,000,000,000.
Then another comment by the writer of the foreword:
Public opinion in our own country is so far sound on the question of currency, but signs are not lacking in some lay quarters of an inclination to sanction dangerous experiments.
Then on page 27 of the book itself, there is the following:
Still another difficulty appeared. There had come a complete uncertainty as to the future. Long before the close of 1791 no one knew whether a piece of paper money representing a hundred livres would, a month later, have a purchasing power of 90 or 80 or 60 livres.
The livre at that time was worth about a franc, or about twenty cents. A further quotation from the same page:
But these evils, though great, were small compared to those far more deep-seated signs of disease which now showed themselves throughout the country. One of these was the obliteration of thrift from the minds of the French people. The French are naturally thrifty; but, with such masses of money and with such uncertainty as to its future value, the ordinary motives for saving and care diminished, and a loose luxury spread throughout the country. A still worse outgrowth was the increase of speculation and gambling. With the plethora of paper currency in 1791 appeared the first evidences of that cancerous disease which always follows large issues of . irredeemable currency,-a disease more permanently injurious to a nation than war, pestilence

or famine. For at the great metropolitan centres grew a luxurious, speculative, stockgambling body, which, like a malignant tumor, absorbed into itself the strength of the nation and sent out its cancerous fibres to the remotest hamlets. At these city centres abundant wealth seemed to be piled up: in the country at large there grew a dislike of steady labour and a contempt for moderate gains and simple living.
Then from page 29:
In the leading French cities now arose a luxury and license which was a greater evil even than the plundering which ministered to it. In the country the gambling spirit spread more and more. Says the same thoughtful 'historian whom I have already quoted: "What a prospect for a country when its rural population was changed into a great band of gamblers!"
And page 31:
Even worse than this was the breaking down of the morals of the country at large, resulting from the sudden building up of ostentatious wealth in a few large cities, and from the gambling, speculative spirit spreading from these to the small towns and rural districts. From this was developed an even more disgraceful result,-the decay of a true sense of national good faith. The patriotism which the fear of the absolute monarchy, the machinations of the court party, the menaces of the army and the threats of all monarchical Europe had been unable to shake was gradually disintegrated by this same speculative, stockjobbing habit fostered by the superabundant currency.
Then from page 50 I quote:
Interesting is it to note in the midst of all this the steady action of another simple law in finance. Prisons, guillotines, enactments inflicting twenty years' imprisonment in chains upon persons twice convicted of buying or selling paper money at less than its nominal value, and death upon investors in foreign securities, were powerless. The national convention, fighting a world in arms and with an armed revolt on its own soil, showed titanic power, but in its struggle to circumvent one simple law of nature its weakness was pitiable. The louis d'or stood in the market as a monitor, noting each day, with unerring fidelity, the decline in value of the assignat; a monitor not to be bribed, not to be scared.
When I first went to France the louis was the pocket money of the people, the 20 franc piece. Then there was also the half louis. I continue:
As well might the national convention try to bribe or scare away the polarity of the mariner's compass. In August 1, 1795, this gold louis of 25 francs was worth in paper, 920 francs; on September 1st, 1,200 francs; on November 1st, 2,600 francs; on December 1st, 3,050 francs. In February, 1796, it was worth 7,200 francs or one franc in gold was worth 288 francs in paper. Prices of all commodities went up nearly in proportion. The writings of this period give curious details. Thibaudeau, in his Memoirs, speaks of sugar as 500 francs a pound, soap, 230 francs, candles, 140 francs.
Considering a franc as worth 20 cents, that would make sugar worth $100 a pound. Then on page 58 appears a comparison of prices as follows:
On the prices charged for articles of ordinary use light is thrown by extracts from a table published in 1795, reduced to American coinage.
This was at the time when assignats and mandats were issued:

I shall not give all the items in the long list that appears on that page. Then on page 54 the author has this to say:
Such were the results of allowing dreamers, schemers, phrase mongers, declaimers and strong men subservient to these to control a government.
The last quotation appears on page 66. as follows:
And, finally, as to the general development of the theory and practice which all this history records: my subject has been fiat money in France; how it came; what it brought; and how it ended.
It came by seeking a remedy for a comparatively small evil in an evil infinitely more dangerous. To cure a disease temporary in its character, a corrosive poison was administered, which ate out the vitals of French prosperity.
It progressed according to a law in social physics which we may call the "law of accelerating issue and depreciation." It was comparatively easy to refrain from the first issue; it was exceedingly difficult to refrain from the second; to refrain from the third and those following was practically impossible.
It brought, as we have seen, commerce and manufactures, the mercantile interest, the agricultural interest, to ruin. It brought on these the same destruction which would come to a Hollander opening the dykes of the sea to irrigate his garden in a dry summer.
It ended in the complete financial, moral and political prostration of France-a prostration from which only a Napoleon could raise it.
And Napoleon did later do so. Anyone who has not read Andrew Dickson White's story of fiat money inflation in France should do so, because if anything would cause one to fear the grave danger of inflation in a country such as this, it is his historical account of fiat paper money in France.
While I believe there is a germ of truth in the arguments for monetary reform, how powerful that germ is I do not know. It is worthy of consideration, but without giving the matter more study than I have been able to give it I should not like, to vote either for the amendment or for the subamendment. The subamendment, I think, is well worthy of consideration, but my suggestion is that it
Loan of $750,000,000

should be left at that, without forcing it to a vote. The mover, the hon. member for Rosatown-Biggar, admitted in his very able speech-and he always speaks ably in this house-that he had doubts about the wisdom of the action he proposed, but he suggested that it be done once only to observe its effects. My fear is that if you do it once to note its effects, there will be a clamour, just as there was in France, for more and more- just as the opium eater craves more and more opium as the effect of the first dose wears off.

speechtext: If the hon. member will permit a question, the bill proposes to raise $750,000,000 for various purposes; would he mind stating why he believes the raising of that money will not cause inflation?

maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UN MATURED SECURITIES AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
Again I say that I do not want to put myself forward as one who knows this subject thoroughly, although I have studied it for some years. But there is one thing I have learned, and that is that the knowledge that one is ignorant of a subject is the beginning of wisdom. While I do not wish to speak too positively, the difference between issuing bonds and issuing interest-free money strikes me as this, that you have to pay interest on the bonds, and the interest obligation acts as a control to prevent you from issuing too much; but when you issue money that does not bear interest, the tendency is to go on issuing more because the cost is merely that of the printing and the paper.
But there is another answer to all this argument for monetary reform. Surely all the wisdom of the ages has not percolated down to rest in this House of Commons. If it were as simple as my hon. friends say it is-I am not saying this offensively at all, because I know my hon. friends are sincere-if it were possible for any country to pay its way by issuing paper money, and spending it, if you like, on public works or to pay off its debt, why has not the United Kingdom, to my mind the wisest country in money matters, or the United States, or France, or any other great country, adopted such a policy long ago? If it is as simple as all that, it would have been done long ago.
But money, after all, is only a token. The best definition I know is that money is a measure of value and a medium of exchange. Its use is to simplify trading. Suppose I want to sell something. Rather than running around to find some person who wants to trade something for the article I wish to dispose of, I sell my article for money, and with that money I buy the article I want. Without such a medium of exchange we

should go back to chaotic conditions. Paper money is not wealth. No country can enrich itself by issuing a lot of paper money. The only wealth we have is the wealth we can produce. Without production we have no wealth at all. The only wealth we have is what we produce from our soil, our mines, our forests and other resources.

May I point out that the proposal to retire debt now represented by bonds by issuing currency simply means that you turn a deferred obligation into a demand obligation. By issuing bonds you promise to pay at some future time; by issuing money you promise to pay in terms of goods and services whenever the man holding the dollar bill presents it and demands for it goods and services. That is an important distinction. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) mentioned another important one, but the distinction I am now making is fundamental, if I may say so. We come down, therefore, to a consideration of the amendment and the subamendment and the speeches made with reference to them.
I should like to say just a word about this new utopia, New Zealand. I shall not say a word in criticism of the present government of New Zealand or of its policies.

speechtext:
I am attempting to do
so through the medium of the illustrations which the hon. member and his own friends have advanced, and I would ask him to keep his place and allow me to put on the record some information with respect to a comparison between the results of policy of the present government in Canada and the policies of whatever governments have been operating in New Zealand, without in any way criticizing the administration of that country. We are told that New Zealand is more or less utopia with regard to money matters and interest rates. Well, what are the facts? At the present time, with regard to New
Zealand internal loans in their own country, their four's of 1943-46 are yielding 4-23 per cent, and Canadian fours of 1943^5 are yielding 2-20 per cent, more than two per cent cheaper money to the government of Canada than the government of New Zealand is able to get from its own people, with all the machinery which has been described by my hon. friends opposite.
We hear, of course, only the good things about other countries. I wonder if those who advance other countries by way of example, particularly when they are other countries of the British commonwealth, realize how difficult it is for a minister of the crown in Canada or in New Zealand to indulge in criticism of the policies of the government of another part of the British commonwealth. It is perfectly all right for my hon. friends to represent another British country as a utopia or a heaven. That is fine. But I can well imagine that it would be regarded as a grave discourtesy on my part as a minister of the crown in Canada to make speeches which could be used in criticism of the government of New Zealand or of any other dominion by their opposition. It would be a very undesirable condition; therefore I limit my reference to New Zealand by that one recital of fact to which I have referred.
