I will admit at once
that unemployment represents a major problem in practically all countries. My hon. friend says it is solved in New Zealand. There again I am embarrassed in trying to discuss it, because I want no word of mine to appear to be critical of the policies of another country.
With regard to the amendment, we are asked by its terms to authorize the governor in council-mark the term, to authorize the governor in council-to raise by the issue of currency and/or credit through the Bank of
Loan of $750,000,000

Canada an amount not to exceed $200,000,000 for public works and general purposes. I take it from the language of the amendment, which does not appear to have been very well thought out in its relation to the whole problem, that the $200,000,000 currencyissuing authority which it advocates is not limited as to time. When we come to the subamendment of the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) a limitation as to time is imposed, but I take it that the hon. member for Calgary East is quite prepared to extend this $200,000,000 currencyissuing or borrowing from the Bank of Canada authority over any period of time, because in no sense is there any time limitation implied.
May I point out, to the hon. member and to those who believe that something of this sort is necessary, that all his amendment seeks to attain is now within the power of the governor in council, if I read his amendment correctly. It is now within the power of the governor in council through the medium of the Bank of Canada. That is to say, if the government wishes to make an arrangement with the Bank of Canada to buy its treasury bills, or if it wishes to make an arrangement with the Bank'of Canada to borrow against expected revenues, full provision for both these ends is found within the four comers of the present Bank of Canada Act. May I point out further that there seems to be in the minds of hon. gentlemen in the corner some virtue in printing more money and issuing that money as against borrowing the money from the Bank of Canada at a lesser cost than is involved in printing it, or at any rate at approximately the same cost. The present rate on treasury bills, which are virtually put up to auction every month and which are outstanding at the moment to the extent of either $150,000,000 or $155,000,000, I forget which, is less than two-thirds of one per cent per annum in the form of interest payable by the government of Canada upon those treasury bills. I speak from memory, but I think I am correct in saying that the cost of printing money exceeds one-half of one per cent, and certainly what is involved in its distribution entails much more than that. So that, according to the terms of the amendment itself, the sole effect of its carrying, apart from defeating the government, would be to alarm the people with the idea that we were going very much beyond our usual financial practice of recent years in financing public undertakings. In effect it would not add one tittle to the authority of the government or to the authority of the Bank of Canada, if I read the amendment correctly, and I think I do.

On the general principle may I point out, following the very pertinent remarks of the leader of the opposition, that in the last ten or fifteen years the world has moved further away from metallic backing for currency than ever before in its history. Always previously there had been nations who, out of the bitter experience of their own recent past, stood fast against getting away from a substantial gold or other metallic backing for their currency. The different parts of the world have got closer together since the great war in matters of finance and economics; and, following the London conference of 1933, a lesser proportion of gold backing is now recognized as being practicable-combined, however, with sound and careful monetary management; that is the essential.
We have moved, then, toward and into the realm of managed currency. Not only this country but practically all the major countries of the world are now operating on that basis. Proposals such as those to which we have listened to-day have a familiar ring, in that they are identical with a type of proposal which has always been heard whenever in the past in any individual country a managed system of currency has been set up. Always the popular assembly says, let us have more money. Always there is some unfortunate person standing as I stand to-day, warning as to the consequences. Why do I say that? In order to try to get away from the evils attendant in the past upon managed or mismanaged currency. Every country having at present a managed currency is, through the medium of expert investigation and consideration of all the economic factors, trying to go carefully and slowly in the direction of building up a large volume of paper money. All history tells us what a difficult thing it is to manage paper currency backed only to a limited extent by metal or other forms of value. Every country is proceeding slowly.
In our own case, I have previously pointed out the extent to which our currency issue and consequently our deposits have grown during the past four years. I have tried to describe the motives which have actuated what I have called our easy money policy and the results which flow from it. I know it is easy to be popular by saying, why not issue more? But may I point out that the very nature of the proposals to which we have listened to-day indicates how little careful examination of the bases is really made by those who propose them, because they are willing to consider two hundred million dollars if they cannot get six hundred millions, and

the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party is willing to consider one hundred millions. No basis was advanced as to why we should undertake to issue one hundred millions, particularly, or fifty, or forty, or thirty. My experience is that those whose business it is to watch from day to day the factors which make it wise or desirable to enlarge by this sum or that sum would be the last to be dogmatic as to the amount which could safely be issued under any given set of circumstances.
The leader of the opposition expressed my feelings when he said something to the effect- I have said it before in this language, which maybe is not quite like his-that the more I know about this vast and complex subject the more conscious I am of my own limitations in that regard. And I go this much further, that the more any man really learns about it, the less dogmatic he will be as to what can be done at a given moment with such a delicate and complex matter as the management of the currency and credit of a country. The factors which operate are ever changing. They are not controlled entirely within even the confine of our own country. Things which happen elsewhere constantly affect what we in Canada can do, just as what is happening here in Canada has its effect upon what other countries can do. I was one of those who hoped that out of the conference of 1933 might come a greater degree of world cooperation in monetary matters. I believe that conference represented the high-water mark along that line up to that time. But everyone knows what happened subsequently. Everyone knows that forces diverse from and greater than monetary forces intervened and operated to prevent further growth and development, internationally speaking, of the monetary question, from 1933 onward. Progress has been made within what is known to-day as the sterling bloc, those who normally associate themselves with Great Britain and the pound sterling; and progress has been made as between the sterling bloc and France and those who associate themselves with her, and the United States. But no one can say what the future may hold with respect to international agreement on matters of monetary management.
I do urge upon this house the undesirability of parliament itself, 245 individuals, attempting by any form of resolution to say whether 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 100 or 600 million dollars should be issued or what amount should be issued by the Bank of Canada. It seems to me that a deliberative assembly-and I say this with all respect to that assembly-cannot 71492-257
possibly judge to a million or even to ten millions or a hundred millions what is the proper amount of currency for its central bank to have in existence at a given time. The deliberative assembly should, as is its right and duty, endeavour to assure itself that the executive body to which it has entrusted its currency-issuing power is using that power in the best interests and for the well-being of the people and the nation as a whole.

I will admit at once that those who originally framed the Bank of Canada Act-and I share their view-did not regard monetary control as all-powerful, as the only factor. We all know, with the exception of the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Landeryou)-I think even those associated with him know-that there are many factors of a non-monetary kind which are more powerful than any particular monetary policy in their impact upon the economic life, of the nation. A good sound monetary policy will help; a good sound monetary policy will assist in preventing undesirable economic developments from arising from other causes. But the mistake of the hon. member for Calgary East, and of those who held similar views years ago at the time of the French revolution, is in assuming that the mere issuance of money is all that is necessary to make the people happy and prosperous. Those who, as I say, held these views at the time of the French revolution, discovered their mistake to their bitter cost; most of them lost their heads, as a matter of fact, not figuratively as my hon. friend does, but literally.
This bill is a very ordinary measure. It continues the borrowing authority to the government, to enable the government to perform one or two essential governmental acts. One is to arrange for meeting the obligations of Canada in the terms of the obligations as they come due. The second is to provide the wherewithal to carry out the instructions of this parliament in regard to expenditures. That is all that is involved in this bill. It does not necessarily involve this discussion of monetary policy, which is really a separate matter. My hon. friends have hung upon the bill a discussion of monetary policy. That is their right.
I shall ask the house, Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the government, to vote down both amendments. I do not think I have any alternative. I do not believe either amendment to be really constructive. I am doubtful if either confers upon the government any greater power than it has to-day. I take it that the amendment to the amendment adopts all the language of the amendment, in that it would authorize the government to do certain things, except that it would limit the amount to $100,000,000, would eliminate the words "general purposes" and would impose upon the authority conveyed under the bill a twelve month limit. I think I have interpreted the amendment to the amendment correctly. If during the coming year a set
TMr. Dunning.]
of conditions should arise which seemed to make it desirable for the government to borrow more largely from the Bank of Canada, that, as I have indicated, can be done. I submit that this house cannot intelligently determine to-day by resolution that we ought to borrow $100,000,000 or $200,000,000 or $600,000,000 or $1,000,000,000 from the Bank of Canada. That, I submit, is a general executive matter which, in the nature of things, must be given day to day study not by only one group of people but by a number of groups of people studying the impact of the various factors of our economy.
I do not think I can say more at the present time; I do not want to traverse ground already covered, but I do ask the house to vote against the two amendments.

I am speaking of social credit, of which Major Douglas is the originator. It has nothing to do with the printing of paper money; especially has it nothing to do with what is always brought in, the unlimited printing of it.
In opposing this bill we are not advancing any social credit ideas. It is a matter of principle. All we say is that if the government must spend money for governmental purposes, then the government should once more assume its sovereign powers and create and distribute its own money. Anyone would think that was a new idea. No; that is the old idea. This idea of borrowing from bankers is the new idea, the idea which has landed this and every other country in a sea of unpayable debt. When did the national debt of Great Britain arise? It began with the rise of the Bank of England. There was no national debt until the Bank of England was created, but that debt has been growing from that day to this. In connection with this bill we are not advocating any social credit concepts at all. We merely say that this is a

sovereign government; that it has the power, which nobody else should have, of issuing and controlling the money of the country. We are not proposing any amount, either $100,000,000, $200,000,000 or $300,000,000; all we say is that if this government finds it necessary to expend money in the interests of the country-we do not know what sum may be required-that sum should not be borrowed but should be created and used, as it always was before the rise of the banking interests.
I should now like to say a word in regard to the French assignats. As the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) very truly said, those assignats were sabotaged. They were based on the land of France, which land up to the time of the revolution belonged to the aristocracy and the church. The land was confiscated from both, and as many of the aristocracy and members of the church as could sought refuge in Great Britain, where they found themselves among friends of all kinds. The English were at war with France, and of course the English bankers were just as much opposed to the idea of the government issuing money as they are to-day. What was the obvious thing to do? What would anybody do, if he were faced with that situation? It was, as the hon. member for New Westminster suggested, the simplest thing. Millions or billions of those assignats were printed in England and sent to France, utterly destroying the French issue. In that way they got back at the revolutionary government, in the hope, of course, of bringing about a restoration of lands. That is the truth about the French assignats.

speechtext:
In order to prevent Germany from paying debts every country had to raise its tariff. I should like to point out that if the allied countries had been operating under a system of social credit they could have accepted German repayments in goods as the greatest of blessings. The debts could have been paid. But under our orthodox system of finance and economics it is impossible to pay those debts.
In reference to the statement of the Minister of Finance concerning the care and, I might say, the infallibility of the Department of Finance in ordering the financial affairs of this country, I would point to a greater chancellor than our Minister of Finance; I refer to Viscount Snowden, Chancellor of the Exchequer in England in 1931. He held office in a country greater than Canada. In Great Britain at that time they were faced with an economic and financial crisis. He took the advice of the same orthodox economists, the same bankers. Their advice was a most drastic deflation. A royal commission headed by Sir George May, reputed to be one of the greatest financial
fMr. Jaques.]
authorities in the empire, was appointed. That commission brought out a report which was endorsed by the city of London-and when I refer to the city of London I mean, of course, the bankers of London. In the report there was the recommendation for most drastic economies. Everything must be cut down-[DOT] social services, the dole, pensions, the army and the navy. That was done, with most disastrous consequences, until the very navy mutinied. The socialist government was forced out of office to make way for a nationalist government, and the nationalist government was elected to keep Great Britain on the gold standard. It had not been elected very long before Great Britain was forced off that same gold standard, to the great advantage of everybody in the country.
When these authorities are quoted to us as being infallible, we look back on events in our own recent history. These very same people are sponsoring the greatest spending program the w'orld has ever seen. Without quoting figures, they are spending to-day what would have been considered unthinkable sums ten years ago. This money is not being spent on consumable goods, it is being spent on goods which the general public will never use. A total of ten billion dollars a year is being spent on rearmament, and surely no one will argue that this is being spent on producing consumable goods. This total of ten billion dollars, not $200,000,000, is all being spent in Great Britain. Does anyone say that there will be uncontrollable inflation, that the country will be ruined? No, there is no answer to that. There is no inflation there. Why? As my hon. friend beside me says, first because it is extremely good business for the bankers. There are no private borrowers. Why not bring the people to a state of mind where they will submit to any amount of taxation? It will then be quite safe to lend money in the sums which they require because the people will submit to any degree of taxation in order to be made secure from a hostile power. That is why the money is forthcoming.
Hon. members opposite laugh at our ideas. They are so dogmatic in their ideas of what is orthodox and sound. They cheer every time the Minister of Finance mentions inflation. I should like any one of them to explain how ten billion dollars can be spent on goods in Great Britain which are not retailed without the evils of inflation. I hope it is not being thought that the people of Great Britain are putting their hands into their pockets to bring out the pennies they have saved. If the bankers and financial institutions of Great Britain can create money for this purpose to lend to the government at interest, I should

Loan oj $750,000,000
like to know why the government cannot create the money to rearm the country without debt, without interest and without inflation. That is what we should like to know, but that is what we are never told. As soon as it is proposed that the government should issue its own money, the orthodox immediately rise and cry "inflation." They ask us to look at Germany and France and the uncontrollable inflation that occurred there.
Every country in the world is doing precisely this thing. The only trouble is that at the same time they are accumulating unpayable debts. If a bank creates money for the people to use, that is not considered to be inflation, but if the government does, that is inflation. That is the only argument the opposition have, and there is no real argument about it. With regard to President Lincoln of the United States, I urge Liberal members to read the book of one of their own members, the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer). I understand that hon. gentleman is an eminent commercial lawyer. He took the trouble to go to Washington to seek out the records and we have his word for it- this is corroborated by many other authorities -that President Lincoln was murdered because he had threatened the monopoly of the bankers who were issuing the money of the country. His greenbacks fought and won the the war, and he would have continued had he been given his way and not been overcome by the power of finance. This is all in the book, Conquest of Poverty, by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard.

I think they will find them worth while. After all, they contain the opinions of members of this house who are supposed to take the most interest in financial affairs.
When you become more familiar with a thing, you lose many of the prejudices you may have had because that thing is new. We should consider the state of affairs in Canada and in all parts of the civilized world. We should consider the economic state of society in the United States, Europe and everywhere else. We should consider what has happened under the blessings of orthodox finance. Is the state of the world such that the people should close their minds to- any possible alternative? The Bank of Canada
does not decide the government's financial policy; the government decides its own financial policy and then carries it into effect through the instrument that has been created for the purpose. That is my understanding of the Bank of Canada. The financial policy of the government for the coming year is indicated by this bill. It is a policy of borrowing $750,000,000, some of it to be used to retire maturing obligations, a part of it to be used for financing public works. My understanding is that the amount of maturing obligations that will be retired this year is

$575,000,000. That would leave $175,000,000 to be used for public works. When the government wants to buy treasury bills, it goes to the bank and declares that it wants so much money in treasury bills, or treasury bills fol a certain amount. We in this corner are asking the government to go to the bank and, instead of requiring the issue of treasury notes, to ask for the issue of a certain amount of new money.
I would point out that we have not said definitely that we want $100,000,000 in new currency. The amendment to the amendment says "a sum not to exceed $100,000,000," and the amendment asks for "a sum not to exceed $200,000,000." We are here on new ground. If this policy were accepted and the government felt that $100,000,000 were too much new money to issue at one time, then, according to the amendment, they would be quite in order, if parliament approves this amendment, in issuing a lesser amount, whatever might be issued with safety. We are on the horns of a dilemma. If we continue borrowing, the day will come when we shall have reached the limit of our borrowing powers; on the other hand, we must borrow or we must issue new money in reasonable amounts to meet the purposes of the government.
I believe the minister said on a former occasion when the same subject was under discussion, that he did not believe $100,000,000 of new currency would cause inflation. I believe that is the amount he mentioned. Within certain limits, those limits to be carefully watched, it would, in my opinion, be better to issue some new money than to be continually borrowing. We must remember that every time we borrow we transfer the right to property. What is being done by our continual borrowing is to increase the property rights of a certain class of people at the expense of the property rights of all the people, so that to-day a small percentage of the people of Canada own the greater proportion of the wealth and resources of the country. Every time we raise money by borrowing we are transferring property rights.
When I was a child I was raised in a fairly strict, but not too strict, Presbyterian family. I was brought up on the Bible. I was continually told of the evil of borrowing. The sad example of Esau, who sold his birthright to Jacob for a mess of pottage, was brought to my attention. Esau sold something which was of material value to him. Every time we borrow we give away something which is of material value to us until such time as we can pay back the loan, but we cannot pay it back, for the very reason we had to borrow it in the first place.

I do not agree with my friends on the left as to their monetary policy. I admit that to-day, because of the enormous power of finance, money is an immensely important factor in our economic life. But I do not believe that merely by issuing new money we can make our economy operate without bringing about fundamental social changes. However, my hon. friends have very good authority for suggesting that we create new money. During the last parliament members heard a great deal about the creating of new money; and when the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Landeryou) moved on behalf of his group an amendment for the creation of $600,000,000 of new currency, he was not so far away from a proposal which was made in this house in 1935 by one who is now a cabinet minister. I have before me Hansard of 1935, and at page 1193, I find, among a number of suggestions for ending unemployment made by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie), who is now Minister of National Defence, this one:
I suggest the increase of our currency by $430,000,000, which is scientifically justifiable by the appreciation of gold values.
That was the talk throughout western Canada, I remember during the 1935 election the last campaign meeting which was held by the Liberal party in Vancouver. It was in the ballroom of the hotel Vancouver; and all the candidates of the Liberal party from the lower mainland, or at any rate from the city itself, were present, and the platform was crowded with a galaxy of British Columbia Liberal stalwarts. The hon. member for Van-couver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer) proposed his monetary policy, the creation of money to finance consumption; he enlarged on it and told of the support he was going to have when he came to Ottawa-support from all parts of the house-and there was not a Liberal candidate on that platform who rose and said that he did not agree with the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard. If they did not rise and say they disagreed with him, surely the audience had a right to believe that they agreed with him.

Mr. T. J. O'NEILL (Kamloops):	Mr. Speaker, it had not been my intention to speak on this matter because I believed the whole thing was out of order. However, the hon. member who just took his seat (Mr. Maclnnis) referred to a meeting of stalwart Liberals in Vancouver. I was one of the Liberals fortunate enough to be elected in British Columbia in 1935. I did not happen to be in Vancouver when the meeting to which he refers took place, but I may tell him that I was in 
complete accord with the views expressed there, and after listening to the speeches that have been made on this subject of monetary reform I am even more in accord with what was said at that meeting.
To my mind the Bank of Canada should have been created to look after the monetary policy and needs of the people of this country. Whether or not it was instituted for that purpose I do not know. Every time anyone rises to speak in opposition to orthodox finance, his ideas are immediately ridiculed. But to-day, Mr. Speaker, we are doing things we did not do ten years ago, and any man who had advocated them at that time would have been called positively insane. If anyone had suggested that money could be borrowed at less than one per cent he would have been told that it was absolutely impossible, yet to-day we are doing that very thing. I am not going to say that we should have more money or more credit; I am not sufficiently versed in the financial system of the dominion to know what we should have. I do know, however, that if an emergency such as war should overtake this country, money and credit would be made available at once in unlimited quantities. There is in existence in Canada to-day an emergency which, in my opinion, is just as bad as war, if not far worse. We have been told from the opposition benches that thousands of our young men are dying of starvation. I cannot agree with that at all, but I do know that in this country, probably the most blessed in the world, thousands of people are suffering from privation of one kind or another.
This situation could be relieved by a change in our monetary system, without inflation. Every time anyone speaks of issuing new money he is instantly met with the cry of inflation. If you want to increase the credit of this dominion and you do so by issuing bonds on which you pay interest, that is not inflation. The instant you suggest that you should do that without paying interest, that is called inflation. I cannot see where, there is any difference in the procedure, so far as inflation is concerned. If one looks in a dictionary to find the meaning of " inflation," he will find that it describes inflation as the issuing of paper money. Well, my idea of inflation would be to issue any kind of money, paper or otherwise, in quantities in excess of the amount required to buy the goods and services produced by the country. If you do not issue your currency in amounts in excess of the goods and services in your country, to my mind you have not inflation, and your money will retain its value, whether

Loan of $750,000,000
it be gold or paper. But if you issue more than is required to buy what you have to sell, you have too much money.
In my opinion we have not too much money or too much credit in Canada to-day. I say that because we have hundreds of people who are willing and anxious to work, but who cannot get an opportunity to work. There are thousands of people who wish to buy some of the luxuries of life, but they have not the wherewithal to buy them. There are many people who are short of the necessities of life because they have not the money to buy them. When a condition like that exists in a country, then to my mind there is not too much money or too much credit. I believe we are out of order when we speak of anything under discussion before a committee, so that I shall not do that. But we are advised by some of the most reliable financial authorities in Canada that to-day we are using less than one-sixth of the available credit of the dominion, a credit that could be used without reducing the finances or injuring the credit of the country in any way.
Mention was made to-day about the absurdity of buying ourselves out of debt. Well,
I think it is infinitely more ridiculous to attempt to borrow yourself out of debt. You can never buy yourself out of debt. I am one who considered that we should have a Bank of Canada and that that Bank of Canada should be publicly owned. I congratulate the government of the day upon bringing about that condition. But if that Bank of Canada does not bring about the monetary reform which it could bring about, then we have only another bank added to the banks we already have, and it will not do us a particle of good.
To-day the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) told us that we are borrowing in the neighbourhood of S155,000,000 at less than three-quarters of one per cent. I am quite in agreement wTith that. As a matter of fact, I do not see how our present financial structure has a possible chance of living unless we do that very thing. If you are going to borrow money it must eventually be borrowed at the actual cost of production. That is the only way the financial structure can live.
No private concern to-day would be given money by a bank on the same terms as those at which the government borrows. If any private industry reached a state where it had to borrow money to pay the interest on what it already owed, that business would not be able to get money from a financial institution. Yet that is the very thing we are doing to-day, with respect to borrowing money and the payment of interest. When any of us wishes to borrow money in excess of the
amount for which the bankers think we can supply security, they will tell us we must get someone to back our note. If a man who borrows money is able to pay back on the note, everything is well and good. But in the event that he is not in a position to pay back, the backer of the note must pay. In any event the banker gets the interest. The man who backed the note is the one who put up the collateral security ; yet the banker gets the interest.	.
To mv mind we are doing exactly that in public financing to-day. When we require money in large amounts for public purposes we issue bonds. Those bonds are sold to financial institutions or banks. When we sell bonds in that way we have to pay an interest rate. But the only thing that makes those bonds good on the money markets of the world is the fact that they are backed by the natural resources of this country. Those natural resources do not belong to the bankers. When we have a Bank of Canada owned by the government, I cannot see any reason why that bank cannot issue bonds, or why without any difficulty it cannot issue currency. I cannot see that, and so far no one has been able to explain it to me. I believed during the 1935 campaign and I still believe that, instead of being a measure providing for $750,000,000, the measure introduced by the Minister of Finance might be one for a billion dollars to relieve distress in Canada; and the great majority of it should be financed by the Bank of Canada, without increasing the debt of this country.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF

speechtext:
I was about to direct the minister's attention to a phase of this bill which I think may be discussed properly under either section 6 or section 8, and possibly I might be permitted to call attention to the matter now. I refer to the subject of occupational training. In the discussion of this bill in the public press and, I believe, in some of the official pronouncements made prior to the introduction of the legislation it was suggested that the bill would cover appropriations for what is commonly known as occupational training. I assume the application of the grant made under section 6, which is payable to any province, will be determined in a measure by the terms of the agreement referred to in section 8, which is to be made between the minister and the government of the province.
I am very much interested indeed in this subject of occupational training. In the city of Montreal I am in contact with a considerable number of young men who come to me for advice concerning prospective training. We have there a number of night and other schools in which occupational training is given to a certain extent. It is a phase of educational training which deserves the utmost attention of the government and of parliament, and I was about to ask the minister whether, in the terms under which these grants will be made payable or under which agreements will be entered into between himself and the governments of the provinces, due attention will be paid to the subject of occupational training.
A great number of young men who come out of our public schools, some out of high schools, are not trained for any occupation, and the difficulty in securing employment for them is that prospective employers immediately inquire as to what qualifications the applicant has and what training, especially manual training, he has received. If I am at liberty to do so, I would suggest to the minister that for occupational training to be effective arrangements should be made, between the various labour unions of the country and industrial employers for a revival of the old system of apprenticeship.
When I was a lad, the boys of every family, no matter how well to do the family was, were expected, as a qualification for their life's work, to be apprenticed for a year or two or three years in some employment based on manual training which would qualify them in the future, in the event of embarrassments or financial difficulties, to earn their living by means of such training and such qualifications as they had obtained during their apprenticeship. If we are to have effective educational training in this country I am persuaded that some amicable arrangements must be made between the labour unions and large industrial employers whereby the old system of apprenticeship may be revived.
At the present time the labour unions, I understand, are not very heartily in sympathy with a prospective increase in the employment of apprentices. The idea seems to be that as the apprentices grow up they will probably take the place of older members of the labour unions. But a change must be made if we are to equip young men for their life's work in industrial employment. With this observation, which perhaps is not directly pertinent to section 6, I would ask the minister to explain to us in some detail the provisions, which are

Unemployment Relief-Youth Training
made or are likely to be made under this bill, for agreements with the provinces respecting what is usually termed occupational training.

speechtext: We do have in the Department of Labour, in the person of Mr. R. F. Thompson, supervisor of youth training, one who is fully qualified to assist provincial officers in maintaining that contact with industry and with labour organizations which, after all, is necessary to the success of these occupation training plans. I should say this, that it has been represented to us from time to time by some of the provinces that the limitation of the appropriations to a single year was an obstacle to their entering upon these training projects. That was represented to us on behalf of the province of Quebec. That is one of the reasons why in this bill we are providing for the continuity of this plan over a period of three years; that obstacle, therefore, will disappear in the province of Quebec in so far as it was used as an explanation of their failure to take up the full quota of $225,000 for occupational training plans. I assure my hon. friend that I fully agree that we should see to it that proper contacts are established as between industry and labour organizations and these plans, in order that the best possible results may be realized. I feel sure that the assurance which this legislation gives that the program will be continued over a period of years will assist greatly towards that end.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: Would the minister be kind enough to tell us about the results achieved by that Mr. Thompson, who knows so much about youth? What is the result or the degree of success of his efforts to have young men get jobs in industry after having followed one of these courses?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
I had intended a little later to place upon Hansard, with the consent of the committee, a recapitulation of the results obtained under the dominion-provincial youth training program during the past two years. This, I may say, was requested by a number of hon. members when the bill was before us for second reading. Meanwhile, however, I might answer the question of the hon. member

Unemployment Relief-Youth Training
for Temiscouata by stating briefly that up to March 31, 1939, there were registered in courses designed to lead to employment, 28,614 men and women.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: Was that for the whole of Canada?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
Yes. These are courses designed solely to lead to employment. They do not include the rural training courses on the Danish model which have been used very widely in the western provinces. The actual total of all who have received some form of training is 117,675. That includes rural training courses, and also physical training courses which have been carried on very successfully in British Columbia and Alberta. But the courses which were designed particularly to lead to employment had a registration of 28,614, of whom 9,239 discontinued training before the completion of their courses. Of the remaining 19,375 there have been placed in employment, 8,029, or about 404 per cent; and those still in training number 5,178. That is the statement as of March 31, 1939.
When the bill was before the house for second reading some reference was made to the experience of the conservation camps, or as they are better known, the CCC camps in the United States. Unquestionably the civilian conservation corps has performed a very useful service in the United States. It would be a mistake, perhaps, to suggest that the whole value of that work is to be measured by the number of those placed in employment. I would equally say that it is unreasonable to assume that the whole value of our youth training program is to be measured by the number of those who have been actually placed in employment. That would neglect entirely, for example, the real service which has been rendered through the rural training courses in the western provinces. Actually, under the civilian conservation corps the placement record is by no means as good as the placement record achieved in Canada with respect to those courses which were designed principally to train young men and women for employment.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: May I say to the minister that the civilian conservation corps camps in the United States are not designed for the same purpose as that for which this youth training legislation is designed?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: As a matter of fact the civilian conservation corps camps of the United States serve a dual purpose. I would agree with my hon. friend that the primary object is wTork, useful work in the conservation of the forest resources of the country. But apart from that there are also training courses.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: Yes, in conjunction with that.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: It is in connection with this that I have stated that the placement record in the United States is not as favourable as that which has been attained in Canada under our training plans.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: The point is that these CCC camps are open to more youth, they are thrown open to practically anyone who wants to go into them.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: That is not quite correct.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: To a large extent.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: No, there is a marked limitation.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
There is a French proverb: "An ounce of prevention is better than a pound of cure." Perhaps it is international 1
There is, of course, unemployment relief. But this is not at all unemployment relief; it is supposed to be for the prevention of unemployment among the youth. A vocation is something most delicate and at times most difficult to find. It is not so difficult to find in respect of manual occupations as in others. Of course, young men who complete a commercial course, or even graduate from a university, are not always ready for life, because there are many gaps in the educational system of this country. In some parts of Canada the commercial teaching is completed by some lessons in manual labour which are very useful for young men. May I say that here in Ottawa, for instance, at the collegiate and some other places, they teach young men how to make good use of their hands by doing some type of mechanical work, or artisan work such as carpentry, and it may help them along. As was so aptly said by the hon. member for St, Lawrence-St. George, in the old times people of good family used also to learn a manual trade in case they might not succeed in their professions. Some kings of France were locksmiths or had various occupations of that kind. This is a lesson of history. We see now these young men who want to achieve something in the world by earning their own living, by being self-supporting, and those who are sure of a shelter, three meals a day, and good clothes, want to have their own money to use, in part for their enjoyment, in part for saving-which is a legitimate desire. Of course it is very difficult for some young men to receive any practical benefit from the instruction they receive under legislation similar to this. That is so for several reasons. In the first place many lectures are attended by young men who do not receive any direct benefit from them
4096	COMMONS
Unemployment Reliej-Youth Training
At times they have to travel quite a distance to follow these courses, and often after having received the instruction they have no money with which to buy the tools necessary to follow any of these trades.
There are many problems facing youth to-day; and if you remember, sir, it was the hon. member for Temiscouata who spoke about the importance of manual labour and the respectability of the trades when this matter was under consideration three or four years ago, either in the house or in the committee. A young man comes to one of us and says, "I want to take advantage of this legislation. Will you please give me a letter of introduction?" This is something that cannot be refused to any young man. He gets the letter of introduction, which he sends to the provincial director. In many instances he receives no word in reply, or perhaps he may receive a reply that is absolutely insignificant and means absolutely nothing. I want the young men to know that we are all interested in them, that we want to do something for them. The political affiliation of their parents does not count; what is important is the future of the young men or young women who come to us for help in finding careers. We are all ready to help; but if we take the trouble to give the boy or girl a recommendation we want it to be helpful to that boy or girl, so that they may learn to use their hands in order to follow some trade and earn some money.
What is the use of boys or girls taking lectures and learning trades if they do not get jobs afterwards, if they do not get any practical benefit as a result? They may be kept busy for a few hours, a few days, a few weeks or even a few months, but afterwards they are not much further ahead than when they started.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: Carried.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: Youth shall not be disappointed. It is very wrong to disappoint the young. I hear a young member say, "Carried." I should like his constituents in the Niagara valley to see how he behaves in this house. Then I am sure none would vote for him, not only the young men but the parents of the young men.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: Oh, yes, they will.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: They might be confused, but if they were not confused they surely would not again cast their votes for him. This matter is too serious to be taken laughingly.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: The technical schools of Ontario go a long way in the matter mentioned by my hon. friend.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: That is a good thing; but technical schools are not located in every city, town and village, so that in many instances a young man attending technical school must pay for his board, and of course in a city or town that is more expensive than in the rural districts. Many gifted young men have not the means with which to pay travelling expenses and the cost of board outside their own homes. Even if they go to technical school and learn a trade they are not always sure of work when they complete their course.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: What would my hon. friend recommend as a policy in regard to the employment of these youths? What industry would be open to them after they received training? That is the question before us now.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: I am just coming to that. I am sure my hon. friend realizes the seriousness of the problem. A young man completes his course at a technical school, either in his own city or somewhere else; he becomes a mechanic, an electrician or a carpenter. How can he get work if he finds the labour unions in his way? That is a very great problem. A moment ago the minister said Mr. Thompson was trying to find some means of establishing a proper contact between industry and the labour unions; at least that was what I understood the hon. gentleman to say.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: With the youth training plan.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
That means two things: In the first place it means that industry must be willing to accept young apprentices, and in the second place it means that labour unions shall not be unwilling to see these young men come in and do work which heretofore may have been done by older employees in the same industry. Therefore either the older employees must show some generosity to the youths coming in, or industry must see to it that new work is provided to engage these young men. It is a most difficult problem, but it is a problem that should be handled precisely by the Department of Labour.
I am not at all sure that this legislation is constitutional, because it relates to education, which is essentially a provincial problem. On the other hand we have put the constitution aside and have said to the provinces, "We are ready to help you in a youth training plan." There was some objection by the province of Quebec in regard to the end of the fiscal year, and that objection is proposed to be met by this legislation. But having in mind what has been done in the past by

Unemployment Relie]-Youth Training
the provincial branch in Quebec I do not know that it would be very safe to sign a contract for three years. These people have not given satisfactory replies to letters of recommendation which have been given by members of parliament on behalf of various young men. We must be sure of what is going to be done, and we must be sure that what is done will be good, practical and useful. There is nothing that humiliates me more-and it must be the same with other members of parliament-than when a young man comes and asks for something and I have to reply, "I cannot do it. I will recommend you, however." He comes again and says, "I have not received a satisfactory reply to your recommendation." I have to reply: "I do not know why. I have recommended you. I cannot tell you any more." He says, "But how is it that your government pays so much money for this very same thing, and yet you cannot get a satisfactory answer?" I hope every cent expended on this scheme will bring satisfactory results to thousands of youth in this country. It is not the number of courses to be followed that counts. We know there are some courses in cooking which are followed by the girls. That is supposed to be taught to girls by their mothers. In Quebec there are many schools of that kind for girls where they are taught housekeeping, and that sort of thing; and it is very good training.
But the best teaching is still the family teaching. There is nothing worse than disappointing a young man or woman; it gives them a very bad impression for the rest of their lives. If this government is to do something, then whatever it does must be done to serve a real purpose.
I would ask the minister to be kind enough to tell the committee how many boys and girls in Quebec have been successful in finding occupations after having taken youth training lectures. But before he answers may I tell him that I know a lady in Ottawa who is a most competent educator of youth-and the minister knows to whom I refer-who told me that 90 per cent of the boys and girls who leave the Ottawa collegiates each year find jobs. I do not see why the same could not be done everywhere else in Canada. If it is done in Ottawa, surely it could be done somewhere else.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: The parliament buildings are only in one city.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
My hon. friend knows
that carpenters, electricians and other tradesmen are needed everywhere. He knows, too, that there are legislative buildings in nine other cities of Canada.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
Answering the question of
the hon. member for Temiscouata, I would say that up to date the total placed in Quebec, including men and women, stands at 524.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
A few minutes ago the
minister said that those who were getting training leading to employment, as he expressed it, numbered about 28,000. The total number receiving training was 117,000, and then he said that, out of the 28,000, those who had obtained jobs numbered about 8,000, of whom about 5,000 are still working. What kind of training are those above the 28,000 receiving? What is the difference in the training received by the different groups?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
As I understand my hon.
friend's question, it relates to the number in excess of 28,000 who have actually received some form of training under the dominion-provincial youth training program. The larger figure of 117,000, which I gave, covered all those who have received under this expenditure, any form of training at all during the past two years. The bulk of the group to which my hon. friend refers would be found in the rural training classes and physical training classes.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: On farms?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: No; these are rural training centres which are established at various points in the provinces which have adopted these courses, particularly Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba. The training centres are formed very largely upon the model of those which for many years have been established in Denmark. Students who are enrolled come in from the outlying farms to a village or town, are billeted there for several weeks, and, while there, receive instruction. They may receive instruction in farm mechanics or Diesel engines. The girls would receive training in various forms of homecraft, and medical training of an elementary kind.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
And then go back to
their own homes?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
Go back to their own
farms, yes. These courses are not designed to draw young men and women from the country to the cities. Rather they are to make them more contented with conditions in the countiy and give them training for leadership in rural communities. That, I believe, is also the purpose of similar training in Denmark.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
On what particular
Danish schools are they modeled?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
I am not aware of the
particular model, but my information is that those established particularly in Manitoba- and in that province Mrs. Lindal, herself of Danish descent, has been active in that work- are based largely upon the schools set up originally in Denmark.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
I do not think so.
From what I have read of them I think they are more like the courses given by the Ontario government. They are very good courses, and I think they serve a useful purpose, but as I understand Danish folk schools, these courses certainly are a far cry from them.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
If my hon. friend ever
has the opportunity I would suggest that she visit some of the schools in Manitoba. I did so for the first time last autumn, and I am bound to say that at the beginning I had some misgivings as to whether training centres of that kind could properly be brought within dominion-provincial youth training. But what I did see convinced me of their great value. As to whether or not they are based strictly upon the Danish model, perhaps my hon. friend is more competent to say than I am.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: I believe the hon. member for Grey-Bruce is right in comparing these schools with the short courses given by the government of Ontario. Has the provincial government of Ontario at any time requested assistance along this line, in view of the fact that it is being granted to the other provinces?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: Ontario has entered into an agreement with the dominion government for youth training. This province has not taken advantage of the opportunity to establish agricultural or rural training courses to the same degree as have other provinces. The bulk of the work in Ontario has been in mining and forestry occupational training, and training in home service.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: Do the schools established in the western provinces-if we may call them schools-get any support or assistance from provincial authorities in the west?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: These rural training centres of which I speak are established under the dominion-provincial youth training program. In the rural sections of Manitoba last year there were about fifteen for young women and twenty for young men.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
May I make a suggestion to the minister? There are courses for everything, but there is one course every young man and young woman should follow, and that is a course in private initiative 
During the last few years they have received courses in paternalism. They have been told that the state owes each boy or girl a job. Of course they have seen scandalous examples in the civil service of Canada, and probably they have seen the same thing in the civil service of all the provinces. On the other hand it is time to teach our young men to follow the example of their parents, and that they should not expect to be entitled to old age pensions when they reach the age of eighteen.
At times I receive most extraordinary letters. I understand the feelings of young men who expect jobs from the dominion government. They want jobs and when we ask them what they can do they say, "everything." "What do you want"? "Anything." There is no one in the world who can do "everything" and who may want "anything." There is the distinction. The best way for any one to qualify for a job is to be willing to do something unpleasant at the start, even at a mediocre salary, and then show that he can do better, gradually, by becoming more and more familiar with his task. That is what was done by leaders of industry in all the countries of the world. Except in Great Britain and in some European countries, you very seldom see several generations of the same family in the same industry. A man will gain a fortune, but his sons and daughters may be spoiled and not interested in his business, and it is finally transferred to others. The dominion and all provincial governments should see to it that our young men and women are taught initiative in order to make successes of their lives. There is a French expression, "une poire pour la soif." These young people must be willing to start humbly. Then they may make progress and finally succeed in their vocations.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF

speechtext:
Are the courses
different in the various provinces? I should like to know the number of youth taking the course in cooking, for example?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
As a matter of fact, a great deal of latitude is left to the provinces in the selection of the courses. The reasons for this are sound. The provincial government is closer to the unemployment situation and the prospective industrial opportunities. A most interesting course in mink farming was
established in Alberta. I saw this course in operation when I was in that province. A number of boys had been apprenticed to mink farmers, and I was told the course was working out quite successfully. Obviously, several hundred boys could not be placed in this way, but as I recall it, some thirty or forty young men were employed on mink farms. When they have completed their apprenticeship, they are to be set up in business, so to speak, with so many mink as partial compensation for the time they have devoted to this course.
4102	COMMONS
Unemployment Relief-Youth Training

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: How many of them were Indians?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: None. They were Albertans.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: That problem which is commonly designated as the youth problem is really part of the general unemployment problem that we have to face in this country. Until such time as we deal effectively with the problem of unemployment, just so long shall we have a youth problem to face. I do not think we can get away from that fact. On the other hand, one cannot help having a great deal of sympathy for the work that has been done by the Department of Labour in trying to establish even a small number of youth in some form of useful work for the years that lie ahead. Even if only a few youth are kept off the streets by performing a useful function, any expenditure is well worth while. However, I think we expect too much from occupational training. A few moments ago the minister told the committee that approximately 28,000 young people took the course in occupational training.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: Training designed to lead to employment.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: Practically the same thing. Of that number, approximately one-third have discontinued their activity. It would be interesting to find out why a little over 9,000 of these young men who were engaged in occupational training decided to' discontinue it. Personally, I would not be surprised if it were found out that they did so because they felt there was a certain amount of uselessness in learning an occupation for which they would have no use later on.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: There has always been a marked wastage wherever education is on a voluntary basis. A moment ago I referred to the civilian conservation corps in the United States. Their record has been substantially the same because they have had many discharges through withdrawals of those who originally had enlisted.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
Could the minister say
whether one-third of those in the CCC camps in the United States voluntarily withdrew from the camps?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: I shall have the number in a minute.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
The arghment I am developing is that many of the trades are disappearing from our midst. When I left school at the age of twelve years I was apprenticed to a

trade and I spent five years learning that particular trade. To-day it has practically disappeared and there are hardly any craftsmen in the trade. The same thing applies to a great many others. The ratio of skilled mechanics to the total number employed in industry is extremely small compared with what it was a few years ago. This ratio has a tendency to diminish as time goes on because of new inventions and new machinery which is continually being brought into industry. When we put a young man into some form of occupational training, the chances are that he will have very little to do once his term of training has expired.
I come now to the other point raised in connection with asking the labour unions to relax their regulations. I do not know that the labour unions have shown themselves to be hostile to youth training, but I do know that they do not want to see the labour market flooded with new industrialists when there is no chance of their obtaining employment. It seems to me incongruous that a lawyer, of all people, should plead for relaxation of trades union regulations. I wonder how many lawyers in this house would consider a relaxation of the regulations having to do with their own profession? I do not think we would find them willing to agree to anything of that kind. I do not, however, wish to stress this point. While I agree with the value of the work that has been done by the Department of Labour in these youth training projects, I do not think we should expect too much in the way of finding employment for these young men and young women. As I said, this problem of youth is part of the general problem of unemployment which we have to face here in the Dominion of Canada. Until the government has a definite policy, until the government adopts a definite plan of dealing with the general question of unemployment, so long shall we have the problem of youth to face.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
A little while ago I gave the number of those who had retired from the various training courses, and I spoke of the civilian conservation corps in the United States and stated that in my belief that organization has had practically an equal number of retirements despite the fact that it provides for wage payments to all members. Under our youth training plan these payments are confined largely to those engaged in the forestry and mining projects. According to the report for the year ended June 30, 1938, the average number in the courses per month during the year was 271,000. The statistics

Unemployment Relief-Youth Training
of those leaving during the year are as follows: sickness and death, 6,862; employment, 48,327; discharged, 23,932; deserted, 48,485.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: What percentage of the total is that 48,000?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: I have not added the totals, but there would be a considerable withdrawal from courses designed to lead to employment.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF

speechtext: Discharges and so on are included in the figure the minister gave?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF

speechtext: My figure also included discharges.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF

speechtext: In the 9,000?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: Oh, yes.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: Would this be a convenient time for the minister to give details of the proposed scheme of scholarship assistance for students on the basis of ability and need, announcement of which was made some time ago, but the details of which have never been given to the house?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
Before the minister
answers, I should like to ask one or two questions about rural training in Ontario. A few weeks ago I heard some groups of young people expressing a desire to have what we call cooperative schools. They feel that the Ontario government is serving very well in providing training in agriculture and short courses in household science, but they would like to have cooperative schools, possibly modeled to some degree on the one held at the Ontario agriculture college last September. Has the minister heard anything from them in that regard?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: I have had no application from the Ontario government requesting that a course of that kind be included in the program for next year, but certainly if such a request did come to us to establish rural training centres in Ontario along the lines of those established in the western provinces we would consider it favourably.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
I did not mean that, that is already being done by the schools in Manitoba, but what I had in mind was the desire of some young farmers in Ontario, both girls and boys, to have cooperative schools established, and I wondered if that could be done under this youth training scheme. I wondered if they had been powerful enough to induce the Ontario government to ask the department here for the establishment of such schools.
There is one other thing which I think might be done; I do not know whether it can be done, but I do not see why not. Rural youth leave Ontario farms, and I suppose it is true of all the provinces, for two reasons. First, they want to make a living, and it is of course very difficult for them to get established on a farm. That is another story. There needs to be some way of helping to establish young farmers on land at rates of interest and on terms of payment they can meet. But quite apart from that, the girls leave country homes, not because they do not want to stay there, but because their parents cannot afford to dress them as they would like to dress, and so they leave and come into the town or city and try to get a job. That reason for leaving will have to be met, of course, by solving the economic problem.
Another reason why young people leave the farm is the lack of a satisfactory social and recreational life. This project of the government might be used to meet that need. The need is for a community centre where young people could meet and get training in dramatics, for instance, with some person who knows how to do the job assisting and supervising them. They also need to learn to sing, and to sing together. The old singing schools of pioneer days need to be revived. These young people also need physical culture training, something like they have in British Columbia. These three things have occurred to me-dramatics, physical culture, music, and I am thinking particularly of singing, as well as all sorts of music. There are many other things that would interest the young people- sports, for instance. I know that the United States has done remarkable work in sending out highly trained people at the request of a community which showed initiative enough to organize with a view to meeting its needs. Then they get some well trained person to come in and help them, and that person is financed to some degree, if not wholly, by the government. That is something we could do. Even if we do not solve our economic problems as rapidly as we should like to do, we could help to brighten rural life all over Canada by helping the young people to develop a satisfactory social and recreational life, and I suggest that the minister give some thought to the possibilities in this direction.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
It seems to me that the training schools, particularly in Manitoba, have done exactly what the hon. member for Grey-Bruce has been advocating. There were two of them, one for boys and one for girls near

4104	COMMONS
Unemployment Relief-Youth Training
where I live, and the program of at least the boys' school included many of the things which the hon. member has suggested. There was singing, for instance, and dramatic evenings. At the close of a course there was even a debate, which by the way was on wheat marketing, and the local board of trade took part in it.
Another thing has been done which perhaps many of us do not fully appreciate. These courses have been designed primarily to give boys and girls in their teens or early twenties an opportunity to become acquainted with and enjoy, if you like, town life; and on the other hand it gives the townspeople the opportunity of becoming better acquainted with the problems of the rural young people. I think the real idea behind it was to give these boys and girls a fuller appreciation of the lives which they were living right at home.
One thing particularly struck me in the two schools which I had the opportunity of seeing. It is true that these schools were largely on a voluntary community basis so far as the teaching was concerned. While specialists from outside were brought in for certain courses, the people in the community also made their contribution, and what has contributed so much to the success of the schools is the calling in of the people of the community to make their contributions. I know, for example, that the ministers in both towns in my constituency made their contribution, as did the municipal officials, the secretary and the reeve; business men, the banker and the townspeople generally, the doctor, the dentist, and the eye specialist all made their contributions to that school. We may think perhaps that this in itself is not very important from the point of view of educational courses for a training school, but my reaction to it was this, that those people made a contribution to the school which they had no idea they could make, which they had not realized they were capable of making. In return they got perhaps a better appreciation of the desires and aspirations of the young people attending the schools than they could have got in any other way.
On the whole I think the schools have filled a definite need, and I could not help reflecting, as I looked at the school, how fine it would have been if a similar opportunity right at our doors had been open to the young people who were boys and girls with me many years ago. It would have been greatly appreciated by the young people who were then just starting out in life. The schools have provided good, practical courses. The instructors have gained

the confidence of the boys and girls, and those attending have certainly taken part in dramatics, singing and many other activities which the hon. member for Grey-Bruce mentioned. So I think the schools at least in Manitoba are providing just what the hon. member desired. Judging from our experience in Manitoba, I believe that the people desire to have these schools continued for a further period.
. Mr. MARTIN: Would the minister consider answering the question which was intercepted, unintentionally I am sure, by the hon. and very eligible member for Grey-Bruce (Miss Macphail).

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OF YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
I am grateful for the suggestion from the hon. member for Grey-Bruce, and I assure the committee it will be considered. I should like to see such centres established in Ontario.
With regard to the question asked by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), the matter of student aid has been brought to the attention of'the government by himself on a number of occasions, and as a matter of fact there have been debates in this house touching the wisdom of establishing national scholarships. Some months ago a delegation from the Canadian Student Assembly presented a memorandum supporting the idea. I told them that I regarded education as primarily and in the first degree, the responsibility of the provincial governments. I did not consider that the dominion government with its present obligations should be asked to establish national scholarships until at least the provincial governments had met their responsibilities in that regard, but I said that we should be prepared to accept projects for student aid within the framework of the dominion-provincial youth training program, which seemed a reasonable method of meeting what, after all, has been a difficult situation for so many young people in these last years. They are equipped to go to university and are anxious to do so, but they have lacked the means, and it would be most unfortunate for this or any other country if, as a result of the depression, we should lose what might come from some of these highly-gifted young men and women who, by reason of poverty or unemployment, or because their families are on relief, are unable to gratify their ambition to go to university. The proposal briefly is this. We have said that we would accept from the provinces a proposal for student aid based on a fixed percentage of the total dominion

Unemployment Relief-Youth Training
allocation to each province in each year, that percentage increasing in each of the three years covered by the present measure. The allowance would be $25 a month for a period of eight months with a maximum of $150 a year, and on that basis we believe it would be possible to give such student aid to 300 students in the first year, 500 in the second and 700 in the third. This proposal has been placed before all the provinces. It is under consideration, and some have already indicated their desire to cooperate.

his officers to prepare a tabulation with regard to the 524 positions that have been awarded in the province of Quebec to boys who have followed the scheme?
