speechtext:
The minister and I
were not talking about the same thing. I agree with the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Weir) that the course would be good. We have very good courses in Ontario running for about three months, but they necessitate young people leaving their homes and going to the school. But that touches the lives of but very few rural young people. What I was suggesting was that every rural community needs leadership and help in developing the abilities of the youth in the community. What was done in the United States was excellent. Where a community of young people-and some not quite so young-are living in their own homes and show an interest in dramatics, they get someone who is well-versed in the drama to come to the community and assist them in bringing out and developing the qualities of the youth in the community. They do not leave their homes and go to a school; the community itself is served by teachers who are thoroughly trained in the art. The community itself is the most natural setting for this work-and I am thinking particularly of the farm. In the evening the young people on the farms want recreation, and they want a form of recreation that develops the qualities which some of them feel they have. I believe that physical training, singing and dramatics
are three forms of culture in which real help could be given where it is needed; but the schools cannot meet this particular need because you could not transplant whole communities and put them in schools far distant from their farms.

speechtext: Have all nine provinces come under the provisions of the act?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF

speechtext: I understood the minister to say that the maximum period during which scholarships would be given would be eight months.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF

speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF

speechtext: Would it not be well to make provision so that even a small number of these young men and women who are in such straitened circumstances could go right through to the top? Take a young man who goes into a forestry training camp in British Columbia this summer. Would it not be possible to give him help for three or four years so that he might become a forestry engineer, going right through and obtaining his degree? If you did something of this sort you would inspire these young people with greater hope. If they are able to go to the top, it means more than obtaining a scholarship for eight months in which they cannot get very far. The same would apply to young women taking a domestic science course. There are many young women who are taking training in this direction. Some of them have marked ability, and if they could go right through and obtain their degrees in domestic science it would be invaluable. I suggest that the minister consider putting the scholarships on some such basis so that these young people can get somewhere along the lines they are pursuing.

speechtext:
I should like to pass a word or two of comment. Upon first reading the clause I felt strongly opposed to the appointment of a supervisor; but I have arrived at the conclusion that perhaps an all-round supervisor is necessary, if one can be obtained to fill the bill. I hope the minister will select one who has some knowledge of industry and some knowledge of employment in the industry. So far this evening we have heard a great deal about forestry and farming. Like my hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George I come from a city where there are many thousands of young men unemployed, with no opportunity of learning anything about a trade or industry, and there is a dearth in training of future mechanics. I spoke of this when the bill was first before the house, and have received from all over Canada letters, both from young men who desire to become trained in industrial trades and crafts, and from employers telling me that they endorse what I said with reference to the training of youth in industry. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George spoke of the same necessity, and on the way out of the chamber mentioned the matter to me. I told him that (Mr. Rogers.]
I had referred to it when the bill was first before the house, and he said, "I endorse industrial training in that regard."
I suggest to the minister that industry be approached, that fifty to a hundred large employers of labour, also leading men in the labour unions-men who know what they are talking about-be called in. At that conference perhaps means could be worked out to put into effect the plan I suggested when the bill was first before the house, namely, apprenticeships in industry supported by the government under this plan, or the establishment of vestibule schools adjacent to industry where young men could be trained in the crafts; for example, those needed in a large plant such as the Massey-Harris, or a large brass manufacturing plant like the James Morrison company, or the Dominion Radiator Company of Toronto, or the Steelwares of London, Ontario, the former McClary company, and hundreds of companies throughout Ontario and Quebec. A competent supervisor should be obtained, a man who knows a great deal more than just about forestry or farming, although they are very important and necessary. So few hon. members have anything to say on behalf of industry or labour that I felt it incumbent upon me to say something about this matter. I am convinced that if the minister called a conference of fifty to a hundred large employers of industry he could engage their assistance in this important work. I do not wish to take up the time to explain how this should be done, although I have had a great deal to do with industry. In this way the minister would assist employers who perhaps are not under the immediate necessity of training additional machinists or welders or artisans in one or another of a hundred vocations. I am>
sure that a plan could be worked out whereby a great number of young men could be trained in industry for their own benefit and the benefit of the country.

speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, May 12, consideration of the motion of Mr. Euler for the third reading of Bill No. 63, to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935.

maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD
subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for a number of days we have been treated to a diet of wheat, with a liberal allowance of red herring thrown in. One of the last doses of red herring was handed to us, perhaps on a platter, for some forty minutes by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) who criticized members of this group and members of the group to my right, but forgot to criticize those most responsible for this policy. This hon. member had a great deal to say because some of us were not born in Canada. I want to tell him now that those of us who were born in other parts of the world are just as good Canadians as the hon. member or any others sitting in this house. I was criticized because I came from Ireland. Perhaps if the hon. member were in his seat I would tell him that the Irish will be found everywhere in the world except one place; and if he is in any doubt as to
Canadian Wheat Board

that he can go to that place and find out. In proof I could tell a little story in about two minutes, but perhaps if I told it to him privately it would be better than telling it here.
We have heard a number of quotations during this debate, and I should like to quote a few lines from the remarks of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) appearing at page 3911 of Hansard for May 11. I intend to quote these few words and then to mention one or two illustrations to show inequalities in my own district. The minister said:
I do not think any member of the house, whether representing the east or the west, can say correctly that the people of eastern Canada, Ontario, Quebec and the maritime provinces-and that includes myself-have not had every sympathy with the people of the west. And that sympathy has been expressed in the most practical way. If my hon. friends will recognize that, we can agree to differ as to whether they are bearing too great a share of the tariff, and I will not enter into a discussion of that question. I might say, however. that if I wanted to indulge in recrimination, I could strike a balance, have a sort of ledger account showing that the west is receiving this and giving that, and so on. But that would be quite purposeless and useless, and it would only tend to cause disruption among us. In my estimation, I could make a good case as to w-hether that 'balance is on the side of the east or the west, but I will not try to do that because that sort of thing only makes for disruption and disunity.
I agree with the statement that when some people are giving more than they are getting, it causes disruption and disunity. In the case of the people who grow wheat it seems that it is more blessed to give than to receive. I have in mind the cases of one or two people in the west who have been soaked, if I may use that word. The first case is that of a widow with several children who for a number of years has been paying nine per cent on a mortgage. The original amount of that mortgage was paid off some years ago, but still more than the original amount remains to be paid. Another case is that of a farmer who borrowed some money, and the mortgage company was so ashamed of charging a rate of ten per cent that it set up a second mortgage to take care of two per cent of the interest and then charged eight per cent on the whole amount.

maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD
subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext: You are not blaming that on the east?

maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD
subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext:
The mortgage company has its head office on this side of the great lakes, as a number of them have. While we were getting a reasonable price for our wheat people 
did not kick so much; but in the present situation, with conditions existing that should have been rectified years ago, the people of the east and of the west as well, I believe, cannot keep out of debt. At page 150 of the report of the Bracken Sonference we find this:
The Saskatchewan brief before the Rowell commission on inter-provincial relations, after exhaustive analysis estimated the total farm debt of Saskatchewan at December, 1937, to be approximately $482,000,000. In 1938 practically no interest was paid on this debt, only half the taxes were collected, direct relief and seed and fodder have been given on a big scale following the widespread drought of 1937. It is estimated that the total debt increased about $64,000,000 during the past year and now stands at $546,000,000 or about $18 per acre of crop land, or about $25 per acre of seeded crop.
We had a price of 80 cents or better at the time this condition came into being, and now we find the initial price cut to 70 cents. With the present carry-over there is absolutely no guarantee that there will be any further payment beyond the initial price. The fact that we are given participation certificates does not at all guarantee that they will be worth any more than the thousands of those certificates that are stored away in the west, and that are absolutely useless at the present time. Since Bills Nos. 63 and 83 have been revised and reprinted, we find that because the initial payment has been increased to 70 cents there has been a reduction in the bushelage, and also a restriction on the amount on which a person may get that initial payment. I am opposed to this provision for 5,000 bushels. If we were getting even cost of production I do not think I would object quite so strenuously, but because the price is far below the cost price I think we have a just reason for kicking, and for opposing the 5,000 bushel limitation.
There is another mistake in the bill in connection with which my colleague from Acadia (Mr. Quelch) received the following telegram from the manager of the Alberta wheat pool: Victor Quelch,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Wheat Board Act section 7 (e) empowers board to determine "place of delivery." Bill 63 deletes those words. Does that restrict it to Fort William basis or can the board under section 15 of act reflect to grower advantage of lowest freight rate whether Vancouver or Fort William as interpreted under old act? Very important Alberta farmer advantage recognized under old act be retained.
Lew Hutchinson.
Chairman Alberta Wheat Pool
I should like an assurance from the minister that we in Alberta or any other province will be given the right to deliver our grain at Vancouver or Fort William.

Canadian Wheat Board

speechtext: I think I mentioned a few days ago, when the bill was under discussion, that it was the practice of the board when it was found that wheat was located farther to the west, which ordinarily, by a shorter haul, would go out through Vancouver, to deliver to Fort William, if by so doing it would make it more profitable; and that in those circumstances the producer would be charged only the rate to the port of Vancouver. speechtext:
I thank the minister. I believe a few days ago the hon. member for Cam-rose (Mr. Marshall), when speaking on this matter, gave an outline of where the farmer was paying his debts some years ago, and where he is paying them to-day. I believe all hon. members believe that the farmer and his family should first of all have their food, clothing and shelter provided, before making payments on the mortgage, taxes or other things. Taxes have a preferred position after living costs, threshing bills and so on. So that perhaps we shall find out that the trend indicated by the hon. member for Camrose for the past two or three years in Alberta will be followed. We hope prices will be rectified, thereby giving those on the land a chance to make at least a reasonable living.
I would strongly recommend the abolition of the Winnipeg grain exchange. We have been told that the Turgeon commission made certain recommendations, and that the legislation up to the present time is in line with them. I am not disputing that statement. I must say, however, that I am not in accord with the Turgeon commission or a number of other commissions set up prior to that time. So far as I can see, the result from all these commissions has been to bolster up an organization which should have been put out of existence a number of years ago. I refer to the Winnipeg grain exchange.
What we wheat growers need is a wheat board to handle our grain. That, I believe, would be the only effective means of marketing. On that board we should not have, as we have at present, members who are not farmers. There should be at least some producers' representatives or, if we cannot have that, we should have an advisory board with a majority of producers' representatives. The pools for which there was provision in the legislation which passed the house last week are an instance of divide and rule, and perhaps accomplish just as well as anything else what the exchange and its friends want. I am opposed to the set-up of a number of small pools, because so 71492-259
long as we have a number of wheat organizations, we might as well have a number of individual farmers selling. We shall never get the results we require.
I do not intend to take up more time, but would point out that 70 cent wheat seems to be the very best that this old, inadequate system can provide for us, and I would advocate strongly that members in the house and people outside the house study the policy of social credit, which would give everybody a reasonable living.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been listening patiently to the discussion on this and kindred legislation respecting wheat, and I have been trying to analyse the situation in the past four years, since the wheat board was first created. I have been trying to find the cause of the situation in which we find ourselves to-day. There is no doubt that there is and has been trouble, right along. I was going to say that ever since this government took office, the matter of the wheat board has been one of uncertainty in the west. There was so much changing that the people did not know just what confidence to place in the board, or the government that was behind it.
One of the first things done by this government was to change the McFarland board to one headed by Mr. Murray. We very soon found out that the advisory committee had been dismissed. At this time I should like the minister to give us a reason for their dismissal. There must have been one. I am wondering whether they were inefficient, whether they were not fulfilling the necessary functions, or what causes there may have been. According to the evidence before the Turgeon commission, Mr. Murray would not accept the chairmanship of the new board, with an advisory committee. The question is whether Mr. Murray was to be the boss, or whether the government had a policy. Somebody had to make a decision, and evidently the government made it and dismissed the advisory committee.
I therefore ask the responsible minister to tell the house why the advisory committee was discontinued, because if there is anywhere a need for producers' committee or the membership of producers on a committee, surely it is in connection with a wheat board. Because the volume handled and the problems that would arise from the growers' point of view, it seems to me-and this must have been apparent to those who drafted the bill-that it is necessary that there should be grower representation on that committee. The

Canadian Wheat Board

board is handling the property of the producers, and when the volume handled is considered, I think the western wheat grower should have a say in the marketing of his commodity. Surely the interest of the grower does not end when he delivers his wheat to the elevator.
To-day there is no advisory committee to the wheat board, which to me is a serious situation. I cannot overlook the fact that legislation has been passed at this session to provide for two advisory committees to deal with producer goods. I refer to the salt fish board made up of five members, two representing the producers and three the dealers and exporters. Then there was an amendment to the Dairy Industry Act whereby an advisory committee is provided for. Is wheat less important than salt fish or any other commodity? Why should not there be an advisory committee with grower representation? I am satisfied that the troubles of the last four or five years can be traced to the fact that there has been no contact between the producer and the authorities having to do with the marketing of his goods.
I feel safe in saying that had this government administered the wheat board act as passed by this house we would have little trouble to-day. A question has been raised in this house, and this question has been of vital interest to the west, as to why sections 9, 10 and 11 were not made operative. Did the government come to the conclusion that these sections would not serve any useful purpose? If they had been made operative there would have been no doubt as to full control by the board from the beginning to the end. It seems to me that this government did not want the wheat board act to function in the way it was intended to function. The other night the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) said that there were two ways to prevent the wheat board from operating continuously. The first was to set the initial payment too high, and the other was for the farmers to refuse to deliver wheat to the board.
Let us look at the record. In 1935 the pegged price was 87i cents, and there is no doubt that the farmers delivered wheat to the board during that year. In 1936 the government passed a regulation whereby the board could not accept wheat unless the price dropped to 90 cents, so we can say that the pegged price was 90 cents. Some wheat was delivered to the board before that announcement was made on August 4, and) I know that farmers wanted to continue sending their wheat to the board, taking the initial payment of 87i cents and participation certificates
[Mr. Needhana.l
which would give them the advantage of any rise in price, but the order in council said that the board could not accept wheat unless the price dropped to 90 cents. The same condition prevailed in 1937. Then we come to 1938 when the pegged price was 80 cents, and the farmer delivered the full amount of his wheat that year to the board. It was not the fault of the farmer that no wheat was delivered to the wheat board in 1936 and 1937. Then we come to 1939 with a pegged price of 70 cents. What do the government say? Do they say they will take the farmers' wheat? No, they do not; they say they will take not more than 5,000 bushels from any farmer. If a farmer delivers one bushel more than the allotted number of bushels, he is to be penalized ten cents a bushel.
The minister said that one of the ways to kill the wheat board was for the farmers not to deliver their wheat. When the producers asked for a wheat board, is it likely that they will try to cripple it in any way? I do not think there is any evidence to show that the producers have prevented the full operation of the board. But it looks to me as though those in charge of the administration of the act have been largely responsible for the situation we have to^Iay. Was the wheat board operated according to the act from 1935 up to the present time? Had that board seen the necessity of creating a reserve, they had opportunities to do so when the price was fairly good. This reserve would have helped to meet the situation we have at the present time. When the price is low is no time to create a financial reserve. The board had opportunities since the act was passed to prepare for the situation we have to-day. I feel like offering criticism for the way in which those responsible have administered the act up to the present time. There have been too many changes. As I did the other dlay, I hold in my hand a petition signed by 10,028 citizens in my constituency. They objected to the passing of this bill providing for a price of 60 cents, and I have had no word of commendation from them since the price was raised to 70 cents. In order to carry out the wishes of my constituents, I must oppose the passing of this bill.

Mr. Speaker, in rising for what perhaps will be the last effort which this group will make to bring to the attention of this house in this critical year the necessity of making an adjustment in the interests of the western farmer, I wish first of all to refer to two or three things which the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) said the other day. He expressed

Canadian Wheat Board
anxiety lest we set an initial price too high and thereby arouse such a storm of opposition from somewhere in the east that it would be impossible to carry on. Up to the present time, except once or twice when we have reverted to the possibility of one dollar a bushel, we have not advocated a price higher than 80 cents. In 1935 the price was set at 87i cents, and we did not hear that the eastern forces were opposing the government policy in setting that fixed price. In 1936 and 1937 the price was virtually 90 cents, and apparently there was no great opposition; at least so far as we know there was none. It seems to me, therefore, that the minister is worrying unduly.

maintopic: TABLE YI
speechtext: Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I am giving the reasons why special consideration must be given to the western provinces, and one of the main considerations is that we are being placed in a position where we cannot possibly survive unless some special consideration is given to us.

speechtext: Not nearly enough. It is contended that Ontario and Quebec farmers are going to suffer a disability. It is contended that they are suffering. I wish to point out, as I have done once or twice before, that we are not contending for one moment that the farmers all over the dominion should not be given that consideration which will enable us to live. When we argue for the wheat industry of the west we are using that simply as a point of departure. The day will come in this dominion, if it is the will of heaven that we find favour in the eyes of fortune, when it will be realized that the men who are engaged in the essential industries in this country must be placed in a position in which they can live, and until that is done we cannot begin to have a sound economic position in Canada. So when we say that the wheat industry must be put on a sound basis we are by implication saying that the whole agricultural industry and every primary producer in this dominion must in a similar way be put on a sound economic basis.

I said "grow," and I mean it. As regards the representatives of the farmers of Ontario and the farmers throughout the country generally, instead of any complaint coming from them with regard to 80 cents on wheat, the thing for them to do is to begin to agitate for a fair price for their own farm products. And it can be given, beyond any question. I have stated two or three times already that if Canada were an island there is no reason in the world why we could not live. Is there any reason? To ask the question is to answer it.
There are two or three other points that bear on the general question, and I wish to put them in a straightforward, simple way before the house in this last appeal we are making. In addition to our having a tariff disability, we are labouring under certain other handicaps, in western Canada particularly, which the people of the dominion must learn to realize and fully to appreciate. Our first difficulty comes from the extremely careless way in which the lands were dealt with in years gone by. In the three prairie provinces there are special areas which have
been seriously affected because of past immigration and settlement policies, which were directly governed by men sitting in this house over whom the provinces had no control.
Take in the first place the question of land settlement. When this government dealt with the Hudson's Bay Company it allowed them to have one-twentieth of the lands from the boundary to the North Saskatchewan river. It allowed them to take sections 8 and 26 in every fifth township, sections 8 plus the south, one-half of 26 in all the other townships. All we need to do is to imagine this floor - of the House of Commons to be a great stretch of land laid out by survey, and allow any group whatsoever to select townships and sections in that way, and hon. members will realize how the settlement over that whole area will spread out in a way which will make it extremely costly to administer that country, no matter who undertakes the task. Not only was the Hudson's Bay Company allowed to select lands all over the country, but the Canadian Pacific Railway was paid in large measure with lands-18,000,000 acres were given them plus the mineral rights. They had exemptions from taxation on their main line properties and twenty-year exemptions on lands and minerals; and by and by more and more lands were pledged to them. Alberta alone was called upon to give the Canadian Pacific Railway 13,120,000 acres of land. The company was allowed to select that land wherever they chose, and once more, the way in which they selected the land forced out settlement in Alberta so that it became widespread. The cost of administering the public services in Alberta and Saskatchewan, because of that mismanagement of our lands, has been so much enhanced as to endanger the financial stability of those two provinces for many years to come.
Unless we realize that, we shall face annual trouble from those two provinces, not because of complaints from the people but because they simply cannot carry on. Practically all the land which went to pay the Canadian Pacific Railway came from the three prairie provinces, and the Canadian Pacific selected odd numbered sections anywhere. They took good care to get the best and choicest lands.
Not only in dealing with these two great companies was the government careless and improvident, but it was careless and improvident in its immigration policy as well. May I read two or three statements which I admit astonished me when I first heard them. I doubt whether very many hon. members have ever heard that such things took place in
Canadian Wheat Board

years gone by. In 1905 the Hon. Clifford Sifton made this statement, speaking in this House of Commons:
So, Mr. Speaker, I am clear upon that point; and if there is anything I can say to the members of this bouse that I think should commend itself to the judgment of both sides, I would say that nothing could be done which would more certainly imperil a successful settlement policy upon which the greatness and increase in the financial strength and resources of Canada depend than, under any circumstances, to allow the public lands of the prairie provinces to pass from the control of the dominion government.
That was in 1905 when the two western provinces were to be set up. Not only had the dominion allowed men to go in and settle at random all over the country, but it retained control over the lands so that the process could go on-what for? For the benefit only of Ottawa, utterly regardless of what might be the interests of people who might try to establish homesteads in Alberta or Saskatchewan.
I have another quotation from the same gentleman:
I want the house to understand the policy which this government is following. It is endeavouring to 'build up a consuming and producing population in our vast western country for the purpose of giving legitimate occupation, without excessive duties, on a legitimate business basis, to the mechanics and artisans in eastern Canada.
This has not been the result of any haphazard policy; it had been planned and designed for many years. We are suffering from it to-day, and we are blaming everybody but the people who ought to be blamed. He goes on:
It is not necessary in order to give that occupation that we should have a fiscal policy which is oppressive to the people who are actually furnishing the money to pay for the goods which are produced in eastern Canada.
There is another quotation, this time from Hon. Frank Oliver:
This Dominion of Canada can make millions out of the lands of the northwest, and never sell an acre; it has made millions out of these lands without selling an acre. The increase in our customs returns, the increase in our trade and commerce, the increase in our manufactures is to a very large extent due to the increase in settlement on the free lands of the Northwest Territories. The prosperity this dominion is enjoying to-day is to a very large extent due to the fact that the lands of the Northwest Territories have been given away and that people have taken them. I say that the interest of t'he dominion is to secure the settlement of the lands, and whether with a price or without a price makes little or no difference. It is worth the while of the dominion to spend hundreds of thousands of dollars in promoting immigration to that country and to spend thousands and thousands of dollars in surveying and administering these lands, and then to give them away.

After the dominion government had exploited those lands as it was designed to do, the problem was turned over to the provincial governments. If a person can imagine anything more unfair, more callous and more short-sighted than that, I can hardly understand his mentality. The earnestness and sincerity with which we are struggling here to-night are to a very large extent the necessary consequence of that very mismanagement.
Not only was the dominion government callous about the settlement of that country, but it disregarded an area in western Canada which has many times been mentioned in this house, known as the Palliser triangle. As far back as 1860 all men who were well informed knew that land would never be fit for settlement; and yet the dominion government allowed people to go in and settle all over that land, building up a problem which would constitute a major burden on the whole Dominion of Canada. And now the wheat bonusing plan through a levy of one cent a bushel, which some of us opposed so earnestly, was apparently designed to place upon the three prairie provinces, whose economies have been so plundered and rendered almost impossible, the responsibility of taking care of the sufferers in the Palliser triangle. In other words, the dominion government builds up a problem which is insuperable for the three prairie provinces and then proposes to leave them to handle it. It is just impossible; that is all. If the members of this government do not realize that and do not listen to those who come here and tell about it, the future will suffer for it. Just how, I do not know, but the future will suffer for it.
Here are some of the results which have accrued from that kind of thing. Alberta to-day has to maintain 500 per cent more miles of highway per 1,000 people than Ontario does, and 200 per cent more than the people of Canada generally. I have read that Alberta must support 90,000 miles of highway.

We do not say that it is any worse in Alberta than in Saskatchewan; I believe the condition is a little better in Alberta, but for either of the provinces it is a crying shame, an impossible condition. The more the people of this country everywhere demand public services, such as schools, the greater the difficulties become because of this widely

speechtext: Social credit.

speechtext:
Social credit, indeed; and if the Liberal party would adopt it they could do it also. It is conceivable, it is possible, for this government so to organize the economy and the financial structure of Canada that part of the price of these commodities can be paid for the farmer, without costing the taxpayers of this country one cent in addition. The question is where the money will come from. The money will come from state created credit instruments issued debt free, and it might be used to remove the surplus from the market, to pay fair prices, to reduce the cost of these 147 items, to establish new projects such as fur farming, honey establishments and so on, or to create price parity in general.
I now come to the last thing I am going to ask the minister in this debate, and I suppose he is not sorry. I am going to ask him earnestly to take steps to see that an 80 cent minimum is given the people this year, that 874 cents or 90 cents be the goal at a not remote date, and that one dollar and not a cent less be the objective on which he fix his mind; for without one dollar a bushel it will be impossible for the three prairie provinces to establish their economy on a sound basis.
I am going to ask one further thing; that is, that the advisory board be restored. The hon. member for The Battlefords (Mr. Needham) pointed out that we have an advisory board in connection with the salt fish industry, as set out in Bill No. 130. Why should we not have an advisory board for the farmers? Judging from Bill No. 82, while I do not wish to be unduly suspicious, I am surely afraid that it was designed to be a casket in which the wheat board was to be conveyed away to the morgue in respectable fashion.
I have one more request, which has been implied since I commenced to speak. It is that Canada provide for a just price on other grain products. I notice that in section 6 of this Bill No. 63 we have repealed section 14 of the Canadian Wheat Board Act of 1935, which section provided for the application of the principles of the bill to oats, barley, rye and flax produced in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. In place of that section we have a provision extending the wheat _ price to the eastern division. I have no objection to this latter; I think the eastern division should have a just price as well as the west, but certainly we must be prepared to apply the principles of this legislation to wheat, ^ oats, barley, rye and other agricultural and primary products.
In conclusion, sir, let me say that we have presented our case in as great detail as time and propriety would permit. We have endeavoured to speak with becoming moderation, but likewise with fitting emphasis. So far as my group are concerned, we now leave the matter to this high court of parliament. For better or for worse parliament must decide.

speechtext:
Hon. W. D. EULER (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved that the house go into committee to consider Bill No. 62, to amend the Canada Grain Act.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT
subtopic: INSURANCE CLAIMS-WEIGH-OVER IN TERMINAL ELEVATORS-GRAIN STANDARDS COMMITTEES- GENERAL REVISION
speechtext:
In section 39 an amendment was made in the committee on agriculture that was not in the bill which went to the committee, changing the section to admit only five per cent of grain taken into the mills to be shipped out. The mills in the centre of the grain district buy a considerable amount of their wheat from farmers locally. When purchasing from a farmer they must take all his grain that he brings there, whether they want that kind of grain or not, in order to keep him as a customer. Therefore in a good many instances they have to ship grain out. Then, again, cars of grain which come there have not gone through government inspection, coming from elevators throughout the country; and often a great many cars ordered by the mill are not according to the grade purchased. There is a one cent per bushel diversion charge on that grain. If the mills cannot use that grain and have to ship it out again they cannot take it, and therefore the elevator companies would not ship grain to the mills unless they were willing to take all that comes to them.
In other instances these mills in the centre of the west often mill low grade wheat for oriental shipment, and in some years past they have milled many hundreds of thousands of bushels. Last fall one of the mills in western Canada, for the first time in a good many years, got an order for some 15,000 barrels of flour to be milled for the orient. The result was that they thought possibly there might be further orders following that, and they purchased 200,000 bushels of low grade wheat. If they had not purchased it then, it would get by them to Fort William, and they
Canada Grain Act

would have to ship it back again. In such instances, if they were not allowed to ship out more than five per cent they would not be able to make arrangements for that kind of business. Again, the mills in the centre have to buy their supplies for a year ahead, and it is pretty hard for anyone to figure out exactly how much and what kind of wheat he would need in the year, because, if the wheat gets by them again, they cannot make proper arrangements for milling.
Back in 1936 when there was a high premium for spot wheat at Winnipeg-I believe it ran as high as twenty-five cents a bushel-the mills were not able to hold the wheat that they had in elevators, because they must hedge on their grain as it comes in there on the Winnipeg market. They had that grain hedged, and at least one milling company at that time had to ship a million and a half bushels of wheat to cover hedges, or they would have lost that premium.
Where the section contains the words "not exceed five per centum" I want to insert the words "except by permission of the board." In other words, I want to give the board authority or power to check over exactly what the mills are doing, and under circumstances where necessary that permission of the board will be given to allow the mill elevators to ship more wheat out. I therefore move in amendment:
That the words "except by permission of the board" be inserted after the word "not" in line 30 page 10 of the bill.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT
subtopic: INSURANCE CLAIMS-WEIGH-OVER IN TERMINAL ELEVATORS-GRAIN STANDARDS COMMITTEES- GENERAL REVISION
speechtext:
For a number of years, until 1929, we complained in western Canada about the habit of mixing grain at terminal elevators. In 1927, 1928 and 1929 the committee on agriculture met here to discuss the mixing of wheat, or the habit that has grown up of mixing wheat in terminal elevators.

In 1930 the act was amended. A new act was drawn up which prohibited the mixing of grain in terminal elevators, including No. 1 hard wheat, No. 2 northern and No. 3 northern. Mixing was still allowed in No. 4 northern and other grades. Since that has been in effect, another habit or evil has grown up, namely, the habit of not mixing at terminal elevators but of mixing back in the country. And among those who have been guilty of this infringement, not the least have been the mills. I say that because the mills have been taking in grain in carload lots, mixing it in elevators, reducing it down to the minimum of grade, and then shipping down to the terminal that minimum grade. They are taking out mill elevator licences. The bill has been changed this year to prevent that habit which has grown up in the last few years. Not only has that habit grown up, but we find that certain of the elevator companies are now building larger elevators back in the country. Instead of 25,000 bushel elevators, they are building 50,000, 75,000 and 100,000 bushel elevators. They are building these larger elevators in order to mix in the country. The board of grain commissioners came to Ottawa this year with the full intention of stopping this habit which has grown up in connection with the mill elevators, and the act was changed in order to prevent this very thing which the mills now want to have put back in the act. I am not inclined to leave it to the grain commissioners to say whether they shall be allowed to ship grain out. I think the act is quite clear that five per cent is enough.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) says that sometimes they get grain in carload lots. As a matter of fact, few if any of these elevators take grain in carload lots until the sample has been brought in. Cars are brought in and samples are taken. The mills take the samples and test them, and then they decide whether they will take particular cars. It is only after they get the samples and have tested them that they decide whether they will take the grain. That is one of the evils which have grown up. For example, 100 cars may be in front of one of these mills. They go out and get samples from the hundred cars, and the samples may show that fifty cars contain grain of the top grades, while the other fifty contain grain at the bottom. The fifty cars of high protein content grain are taken by the mill, while the other fifty cars are shipped on to the head of the lakes. They skim off the best of the protein wheat and ship it across the line, while the other fifty cars are allowed to go through the ordinary channels of trade to

Canada Grain Act
export. When there is a shortage of protein wheat in the United States, a great deal of this is taken away, but this has not been the case so much in the last year or two. In other years, however, it has been done to a large extent. I object to interfering with the act as it is at the present time. This matter was discussed in the committee; we were satisfied to leave it as it is now, and I am ready to vote to do that.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to speak for only a few moments in regard to the question before the committee. I certainly would not want to place any obstruction in the way of the milling industry of Canada because that industry forms a valuable part of the industrial life of this country and is no doubt an asset to Canada. But I should like to say a word with regard to mixing. I was a member of the committee, and I took a stand against opening the door to allow mixing of any kind in connection with our four top grades. It is true that the majority of the committee was against this, but I voted against mixing. I took the stand that it was a retrograde step. We grade every other farm product and try to put something on the market a little better than our competitors, but we except wheat. For the life of me I cannot understand why we should except this main product of our agriculturists. Nature has endowed us with advantages over every other wheat producing country, and we are able to produce the most highly sought after product in the world. Yet we allow our top grades to be adulterated with inferior grades, and this seems to me to be standing in our own light.
As the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly) has said, we allow the United States millers to come over here and skim off our high protein content wheat. The Canadian millers are allowed to do likewise. I do not want to take away any legitimate advantages from the milling companies of Canada, but the fact is that this practice is hurting
the standard of our grain in the old country which, after all, is one of our most important markets. They know these practices are occurring in this country and they know they are playing second fiddle to the millers of Canada and the United States. We cannot fool them. Our best grades are being skimmed off. The board of grain commissioners are allowing the terminal elevators to take tough grades of wheat to mix with the drier grades, and there is no doubt in my mind that the standard is being lowered. The old country millers know this, and this is hurting our market.
I want to say something to-night about how we suffer in western Canada because of a lack of industries. This is one of our greatest handicaps. We have not industries such as they have in the east, which provide the eastern farmer with a market for his farm products.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT
subtopic: INSURANCE CLAIMS-WEIGH-OVER IN TERMINAL ELEVATORS-GRAIN STANDARDS COMMITTEES- GENERAL REVISION
speechtext: They have been killed by a free trade policy.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT
subtopic: INSURANCE CLAIMS-WEIGH-OVER IN TERMINAL ELEVATORS-GRAIN STANDARDS COMMITTEES- GENERAL REVISION
speechtext:
At one time there were many flour mills scattered throughout western Canada. There were many small and large mills scattered throughout the three prairie provinces, but they are gradually being absorbed by the larger companies or closed down entirely. We are losing an industry which is native to that part of the country. The raw material is right at hand, and the cheapest power in the world is available as well as all kinds of labour, but what do we find? I should like to give one example of what happened in my own city of Portage la Prairie. The Lake of the Woods Milling Company opened a mill there forty-five years ago, with a capacity, I believe, of 1,000 barrels a day. This mill has been kept right up to date, but two years ago they decided to close it because their export sales had decreased. They found they could pay bigger dividends by closing up that mill and transferring the business to Ontario. Forty families in that city were thrown on their own resources. The ministerial association took up the matter and some families were placed on relief. I am willing to admit that a few employees were superannuated, but forty families had to be taken care of.
It seems to me that the government of Canada should not allow such practices to occur. Here was an industry which had been bonused or protected to the extent of 50 cents a barrel. They took the farmers' wheat, and ground it into flour. The flour was sent to Fort William, the farmer paying the freight. With that protection, it seems to me that an industry native to the district should be made to see that they owe something to the
Canada Grain Act

people of this country. They should not be allowed to continue to make large dividends and then, when times are slack, take it out of their employees. That is just what they did. I submit this government should say to the Lake of the Woods Milling Company, "You open that mill at Portage la Prairie or else we will expropriate it and sell or lease it to some cooperative company that will continue to operate with more regard for the people and less regard for dividends."

If we have any confidence at all in the board of grain commissioners, it would be perfectly safe to say " except by permission of the board." I am quite sure they would not abuse it; it is in the interests of the millers as well, and should be accepted.
